◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Big-O is THE language of algorithm efficiency. Whether you're writing the Parcel Service routing algorithm, optimizing search, or just understanding why one approach is faster than another, you need Big-O. Section C3 of the PA explicitly requires you to document time and space complexity for every major function — and the rubric grades whether your analysis is CORRECT, not just whether it's present. Master Big-O and the analysis section becomes a 30-minute task instead of a multi-day struggle.

What Big-O measures

DEFINITION
f(n) = O(g(n)) means there exist constants c > 0 and n₀ ≥ 0 such that:
  f(n) ≤ c · g(n) for all n ≥ n₀

In English: f doesn't grow faster than g — ignoring constants and small inputs.

Big-O is an UPPER BOUND on growth rate. Saying "this is O(n²)" means "in the worst case, runtime grows AT MOST as fast as n²." It doesn't mean runtime EQUALS n² — it could be faster.

The big idea: ignore the unimportant

TWO SIMPLIFICATION RULES
Rule 1: Drop constant factors.
  O(3n) → O(n)
  O(100·n²) → O(n²)

Rule 2: Drop lower-order terms.
  O(n² + n) → O(n²)
  O(n³ + 100·n² + 1000) → O(n³)

What survives: the highest-order term, with no constants.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Simplify these
1
5n³ + 100n² + 7n + 1000 → drop constants and lower terms → O(n³).
📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
2
2n + 3 log n + 1 → 2n dominates log n → drop constant → O(n).
3
n log n + n → n log n dominates → O(n log n).
4
1000 → constant → O(1).

Time vs space complexity

TWO INDEPENDENT DIMENSIONS
Time complexity: how runtime grows with input size.
Space complexity: how memory usage grows with input size.

Both analyzed with Big-O, but they're INDEPENDENT — fast in time can be slow in space and vice versa.

For the Parcel Service PA, you must report BOTH for each function.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Trade time for space
# Without cache: O(2^n) time, O(n) space (call stack)
def fib_slow(n):
 if n < 2: return n
 return fib_slow(n-1) + fib_slow(n-2)

# With cache: O(n) time, O(n) space (cache + stack)
def fib_fast(n, cache={}):
 if n in cache: return cache[n]
 if n < 2: return n
 cache[n] = fib_fast(n-1) + fib_fast(n-2)
 return cache[n]

# Iterative: O(n) time, O(1) space
def fib_iter(n):
 a, b = 0, 1
 for _ in range(n):
 a, b = b, a + b
 return a

Three implementations of Fibonacci with three different time/space trade-offs.

Computing Big-O from code

THE FOUR RULES
Sequential statements: SUM the complexities (collapses to the highest).
Nested loops: MULTIPLY the complexities.
Conditionals (if/else): take the WORST branch.
Function calls: substitute the function's Big-O.
Recursion: derive a recurrence and solve.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Multiple blocks
def f(arr):
 n = len(arr)
 # Block 1: O(n)
 for x in arr:
 print(x)
 # Block 2: O(n²)
 for i in range(n):
 for j in range(n):
 print(arr[i], arr[j])
1
Block 1: O(n).
2
Block 2: nested → n × n = O(n²).
3
Sequential: O(n) + O(n²) = O(n²) (drop lower term).

Best, average, worst case

THREE CASES
Best case: most favorable input → fastest possible runtime
Average case: typical (random) input → expected runtime
Worst case: most adversarial input → slowest possible runtime

Most analysis defaults to WORST case — gives a guarantee.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Linear search cases

Searching arr = [3, 5, 2, 7, 4] for target.

Best
target = 3 (first element). 1 comparison. O(1).
Average
target uniformly random. Expected position n/2. O(n).
Worst
target = 4 (last) or absent. n comparisons. O(n).

Big-Omega and Big-Theta

THREE NOTATIONS
Big-O (O) — UPPER BOUND. f grows AT MOST as fast as g.
Big-Omega (Ω) — LOWER BOUND. f grows AT LEAST as fast as g.
Big-Theta (Θ) — TIGHT BOUND. Both upper and lower (Θ = O ∩ Ω).

The asymptotic perspective

BIG-O IS ASYMPTOTIC
Big-O describes behavior as n → ∞. For SMALL n, Big-O can be misleading.

Insertion sort is O(n²) but BEATS quicksort O(n log n) for n < ~30.
Why? Constant factors. Big-O drops them, but they dominate for small n.

This is why hybrid sorts (Timsort, Introsort) switch to insertion sort for small subarrays.
For the Parcel Service PA (n = 40 packages), constants don't matter much. Pick clarity over micro-optimization.

What to put in your PA Section C3 write-up

SECTION C3 LANGUAGE TEMPLATE
For the routing algorithm:
  "Time: O(n²) where n is the number of packages assigned to a truck. The outer loop iterates n times; the inner search for nearest neighbor scans up to n remaining packages. For a 16-package truck, this yields ~256 comparisons — completes in microseconds."

For the hash table:
  "Time: O(1) average for insert, lookup, and remove (assuming uniform hashing). Worst case O(n) under heavy collisions, but the load factor is kept below 0.75 to prevent this."

For the load_packages function:
  "Time: O(n) where n is the number of packages — one pass through the CSV, one O(1) hash insert per package."

Total program: dominated by routing → O(n²).
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Saying "Big-O of n is just n." Always wrap in O(): O(n).

Forgetting to drop constants: write O(n), NOT O(3n).

Forgetting to drop lower-order terms: O(n²), NOT O(n² + n).

Confusing time with space — they're separate.

Mixing up best/average/worst — specify which one you mean.

Skipping space complexity in the PA write-up — required.

Reporting overall Big-O without showing the breakdown — Section C3 wants per-function detail.

★ ON THE PA AND OA

"Simplify O(3n² + 5n + 100)" → O(n²).

"Big-O of nested loops?" → multiply.

"Difference between O, Ω, Θ?" → upper / lower / tight bound.

"Time vs space?" → independent dimensions; analyze both.

"Best/avg/worst of linear search?" → O(1) / O(n) / O(n).

For the PA: document Big-O for EVERY major function, not just overall.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Big-O = asymptotic upper bound on growth rate
  • Drop constants and lower-order terms
  • Sequential = sum (take max), nested = multiply, conditional = worst branch
  • Time and space complexity are independent — analyze both
  • Big-Omega = lower bound; Big-Theta = tight bound
  • Three cases: best, average, worst — usually report worst
  • Big-O is asymptotic; for SMALL n, constants matter
  • For PA Section C3: document Big-O per function with explicit reasoning
★ ON THE OA / PA — WATCH FOR

Big-O = worst-case upper bound; drop constants and lower-order terms. The OA asks you to reduce an expression and to state a data structure's complexity. Also know Ω (lower bound) and Θ (tight bound) exist.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
T(n) = 4n^2 + 100n + 7  ->  O(n^2)
T(n) = 2n + log n        ->  O(n)

Result: keep the dominant term only

As n grows the largest term dominates; constants never change the class. Reducing an expression to its Big-O is a guaranteed item.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Recognizing common complexity classes lets you predict scaling behavior at a glance. The PA write-up requires you to identify which class each function falls into and discuss what that means for scaling. Master the hierarchy and you can answer "would this still work for 10x or 100x packages?" without doing any calculation.

The complexity hierarchy

SLOWEST → FASTEST GROWING (best → worst)
O(1) < O(log n) < O(√n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(n³) < O(2^n) < O(n!)

Key takeaways from this table:

  • O(log n) barely grows. n = 1M means log n = 20.
  • O(n²) explodes fast: n = 10K is already 100M operations.
  • O(2^n) is intractable past n ≈ 30-40.
  • O(n!) is intractable past n ≈ 12.
  • For Parcel Service n = 40, even O(n²) is trivial (1,600 ops).

O(1) — constant time

CONSTANT TIME EXAMPLES
Array element access by index: arr[i]
Hash table get/put (average): map[key]
Stack push/pop, queue enqueue/dequeue
Returning a value, comparing two numbers

O(1) does NOT mean "fast" — it means "doesn't grow with n." A constant operation could be 1 ns or 1 hour, but the time stays the same as input grows.

O(log n) — logarithmic

LOGARITHMIC INTUITION
log₂(n) = "how many times can you halve n before reaching 1?"

log₂(1024) = 10
log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20
log₂(1,000,000,000) ≈ 30

Doubling n only adds ONE step. That's why O(log n) is so powerful.

Big-O hides the log's base because log_a(n) and log_b(n) differ only by a constant factor (Big-O drops constants).

O(n) — linear

Single pass through the data. Examples: linear search, computing a sum, finding the max.

O(n log n) — linearithmic

Slightly worse than linear. Common for "good" sorts and divide-and-conquer.

CLASSIC O(n log n) ALGORITHMS
Merge sort, heap sort, quicksort (average)
Building a heap from n elements (Floyd's algorithm: O(n))
Dijkstra's shortest path with a binary heap
FFT (Fast Fourier Transform)

O(n²) — quadratic

Two nested loops over the same data. Acceptable for small n (like Parcel Service n = 40), painful past n ≈ 10,000.

CLASSIC O(n²) ALGORITHMS
Bubble sort, selection sort, insertion sort
Nearest-neighbor TSP heuristic (for n cities)
Checking all pairs in a list
Naive string match

O(2^n) and O(n!) — exponential and factorial

THE INTRACTABILITY LINE
Polynomial (n, n², n³...) is generally TRACTABLE for moderate n.
Exponential (2^n, n!) is generally INTRACTABLE — even small n becomes hopeless.

This boundary defines the famous P vs NP question in CS theory.

Brute-force TSP would visit n! permutations of 40 cities = 8 × 10⁴⁷ — far beyond any computer's ability. THAT'S why Parcel Service needs a heuristic like nearest-neighbor.

Parcel Service PA scaling discussion (Section C4)

SCALABILITY LANGUAGE TEMPLATE
"The current algorithm is O(n²) where n is the number of packages per truck. For the Parcel Service data set (n = 40, max 16 per truck), this is trivially fast. Scaling considerations:

  100 packages: 100² = 10,000 distance comparisons per truck — still < 1 second.
  1,000 packages: 1M comparisons per truck — manageable, ~1 second.
  10,000 packages: 100M comparisons per truck — would take seconds to minutes.

At 100K+ packages, switch to a more sophisticated algorithm (2-opt local search, simulated annealing, or genetic algorithm)."

The "good enough" principle

For the Parcel Service PA, you don't need the OPTIMAL algorithm. Nearest-neighbor (O(n²)) gives a route under 140 miles, which passes the rubric. Don't over-engineer with branch-and-bound or genetic algorithms — they add code complexity without changing your grade.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Saying "O(n) is fast" — depends on n and the constant. Sometimes O(log n) hash misses are slower than O(n) array scans for small n.

Saying "log n grows fast" — backwards. log n grows VERY SLOWLY.

Confusing O(n²) with O(2n²) — both are O(n²) (drop constants).

Saying "O(2^n) and O(n!) are equivalent" — n! grows MUCH faster.

Forgetting to discuss scaling in the PA — Section C4 wants this.

★ ON THE PA AND OA

Memorize the hierarchy: 1 < log n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2^n < n!

Recognize binary search → O(log n), nested loops → O(n²), divide-and-conquer → O(n log n).

For Parcel Service scaling: O(n²) → "would scale to ~10K packages reasonably."

NN heuristic vs brute-force TSP: O(n²) vs O(n!) is the whole reason Parcel Service uses heuristics.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Hierarchy (memorize): O(1) < log n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2^n < n!
  • O(1) = constant — doesn't grow with input
  • O(log n) is incredibly slow growth — n = 1B → just 30 ops
  • O(n²) explodes fast — n = 10K → 100M ops
  • O(2^n), O(n!) intractable past tiny inputs
  • Parcel Service NN routing is O(n²) — fine for n = 40
  • Brute-force TSP = O(n!) — completely infeasible past n ≈ 12
  • For PA Section C4: discuss scaling explicitly with concrete n values
★ ON THE OA / PA — WATCH FOR

Memorize the ladder and a canonical example for each: O(1) hash lookup, O(log n) binary search / balanced-tree op, O(n) scan, O(n log n) merge/heap sort, O(n²) nested loops, O(2ⁿ) subset enumeration.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n) < O(n!)

Result: know the ordering + an example each

The OA gives a scenario and asks its class, or asks you to rank classes; pairing each with a familiar algorithm cements it.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

For the C950 PA, you must analyze your OWN code — not just memorize standard algorithm complexities. This means tracing nested loops, sequential operations, and recursion to derive Big-O. This section gives you the mechanical tools to look at any function and report its complexity correctly. These are exactly the skills evaluators check in your Section C3 write-up.

Single loops

for i in range(n): # n iterations
 do_something() # O(1) per iteration

Total: n × O(1) = O(n).

Two nested loops, same range

for i in range(n):
 for j in range(n):
 do_something()

n × n = O(n²).

Three nested loops

for i in range(n):
 for j in range(n):
 for k in range(n):
 do_something()

n × n × n = O(n³).

Triangular nested loops

for i in range(n):
 for j in range(i, n): # only n-i iterations
 do_something()
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why triangular is still O(n²)
1
i = 0: inner runs n times.
📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
2
i = 1: inner runs n − 1 times.
3
...
4
i = n − 1: inner runs 1 time.
5
Total: n + (n−1) + (n−2) + ... + 1 = n(n+1)/2 ≈ n²/2.
✓
Big-O: drop the constant 1/2 → O(n²).

Halving loops (logarithmic)

i = n
while i > 1:
 i = i // 2 # halves each iteration
 do_something()

Halving until 1 takes log₂(n) iterations → O(log n). Used in binary search.

Doubling loops (also logarithmic)

i = 1
while i < n:
 i = i * 2
 do_something()

Doubling until n also takes log₂(n) → O(log n).

Loop with logarithmic inner work

for i in range(n): # n iterations
 j = n
 while j > 1:
 j = j // 2 # log n iterations

n × log n = O(n log n). The shape of merge sort and heap sort.

Sequential blocks

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Independent sequential loops
for i in range(n): # O(n)
 print(i)
for i in range(n): # O(n²)
 for j in range(n):
 print(i, j)
1
Block 1: O(n).
2
Block 2: O(n²).
3
Total: O(n + n²) = O(n²) (drop lower-order term).

Loops with different sizes

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Different-size loops
for i in range(n):
 for j in range(m): # m iterations, NOT n
 do_something()
1
n × m operations.
2
Big-O: O(n · m).
⚠
If m is bounded by a constant (e.g., m ≤ 16 for truck capacity), this collapses to O(n).

Conditionals — take the worst branch

if condition:
 # Block A: O(n)
 for i in range(n):
 do_something()
else:
 # Block B: O(n²)
 for i in range(n):
 for j in range(n):
 do_something()

Worst case: take the slower branch → O(n²).

Recursion: derive a recurrence

RECURRENCE TEMPLATE
T(n) = (cost of recursive calls) + (cost of work at this level)
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Linear recursion
def factorial(n):
 if n <= 1: return 1
 return n * factorial(n - 1) # 1 recursive call on (n-1)
1
T(n) = T(n − 1) + O(1).
2
Expand: T(n) = T(n − 2) + O(1) + O(1) = ... = n · O(1).
✓
O(n) time. Also O(n) space (call stack depth).
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Binary search
def binary_search(arr, target, lo, hi):
 if lo > hi: return -1
 mid = (lo + hi) // 2
 if arr[mid] == target: return mid
 if arr[mid] < target:
 return binary_search(arr, target, mid + 1, hi)
 return binary_search(arr, target, lo, mid - 1)
1
T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) — one recursive call on half-size.
2
Halving log n times → O(log n) time.
3
Space: O(log n) call stack (recursive). Iterative version is O(1) space.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Merge sort
def merge_sort(arr):
 if len(arr) <= 1: return arr
 mid = len(arr) // 2
 left = merge_sort(arr[:mid]) # 2 recursive calls
 right = merge_sort(arr[mid:]) # on n/2-size
 return merge(left, right) # O(n) merge step
1
T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + O(n).
2
By Master Theorem: O(n log n).
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Naive Fibonacci
def fib(n):
 if n < 2: return n
 return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) # 2 calls on near-full input
1
T(n) = T(n − 1) + T(n − 2) + O(1) ≈ 2·T(n − 1).
2
Doubles each step → O(2^n). Disastrous for n > 30.

Common recurrence cheat sheet

PATTERN → COMPLEXITY
T(n) = T(n−1) + O(1) → O(n) (linear recursion)
T(n) = T(n−1) + O(n) → O(n²) (insertion sort)
T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) → O(log n) (binary search)
T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n) (partial sums divide-and-conquer)
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n log n) (merge sort)
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1) → O(n) (linear-time tree problems)
T(n) = 2T(n−1) + O(1) → O(2^n) (naive Fibonacci)

Parcel Service PA function-by-function analysis

YOUR PA FUNCTIONS BY COMPLEXITY
HashTable.insert / lookup / remove: O(1) average, O(n) worst
HashTable._resize: O(n) (rare)
load_packages(filename): O(n) — single CSV pass
load_distances(filename): O(V²) where V = number of addresses
nearest_neighbor(truck): O(n²) per truck
simulate_day(): O(n²) total (3 trucks, each O(n²))
get_status_at_time(package, time): O(1) — just compares timestamps
run_cli(): O(n) per "show all" query

Overall program: O(V² + n²) — dominated by routing for the Parcel Service data.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Counting outer loop iterations only — missing the inner work.

Treating triangular loops as O(n) when they're O(n²) (just with a smaller constant).

Forgetting that recursion adds O(call-depth) space.

Saying "if has 2 branches, it's O(2)" — conditionals don't multiply complexity, they pick the worst branch.

Confusing m and n in different-size loops.

Ignoring early returns when computing best/average/worst.

★ ON THE PA AND OA

Single loop = O(n). Nested over same data = O(n²).

Halving or doubling = O(log n).

Loop with log n inner = O(n log n).

Sequential blocks: ADD then drop lower-order.

For recursion: write a recurrence relation, then look it up in the cheat sheet.

For PA Section C3: include the analysis REASONING, not just the answer.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Single loop = O(n); nested = O(n²); triple = O(n³)
  • Triangular nested loops are STILL O(n²) (constant changes)
  • Halving / doubling loops = O(log n)
  • Loop × log inner = O(n log n)
  • Sequential blocks: ADD, then drop lower-order
  • Conditionals: pick the worst branch
  • Recursion: derive recurrence T(n), solve via Master Theorem or expansion
  • Recursion uses O(call-depth) space
  • For C950 PA: analyze every major function, document in Section C3
★ ON THE OA / PA — WATCH FOR

Nested loops multiply; sequential loops add; a loop that halves/doubles the index is log n. Recurrences: divide-and-conquer that splits in half and does linear merge work is O(n log n) (Master Theorem).

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
for i in range(n):        # n
    j = n
    while j > 1: j //= 2  # log n each
# total n * log n

Result: n outer × log n inner → O(n log n)

Reading loop structure gives the class directly; a dividing inner loop contributes a log factor. This trace pattern recurs on the OA.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The greedy nearest-neighbor algorithm is THE most common choice for the Parcel Service PA routing. Understanding when greedy works (and when it fails) is half the battle for Section D and Section F of your write-up. This section gives you both the conceptual foundation and the specific language to defend your nearest-neighbor choice.

The greedy strategy

DEFINITION
A greedy algorithm makes the LOCALLY OPTIMAL choice at each step, hoping that local choices lead to a globally good solution.

No backtracking: once a choice is made, it's never reconsidered.
No look-ahead: only the current state is examined.

When greedy works (and when it doesn't)

GREEDY-FRIENDLY PROBLEMS
Optimal substructure: optimal solution contains optimal subsolutions.
Greedy choice property: locally optimal choice leads to globally optimal solution.

When BOTH hold, greedy is provably optimal.
When only optimal substructure holds, greedy gives a HEURISTIC (good but not optimal).

Provably optimal greedy algorithms

AlgorithmGreedy choice
Dijkstra's shortest pathPick nearest unvisited vertex
Kruskal's MSTPick smallest edge not creating cycle
Prim's MSTPick cheapest edge crossing the tree
Huffman codingCombine two least-frequent symbols
Activity selectionPick activity ending earliest

Greedy as heuristic (when it's NOT optimal)

CLASSIC GREEDY HEURISTICS
Nearest-neighbor TSP: visit closest unvisited city. ~25% over optimal on average.
First-fit bin packing: place item in first bin that fits.
Greedy graph coloring: assign smallest unused color.
Greedy knapsack (fractional): pick highest value/weight ratio. (For 0/1 knapsack, NOT optimal.)

Counterexample — when greedy fails

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Coin change with [1, 5, 10, 25] cents

Greedy: always pick the largest coin ≤ remaining. Make 30 cents.

1
Pick 25¢ → remaining 5¢. Pick 5¢ → done. Total: 2 coins. ✓ optimal.
📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

Now consider denominations [1, 6, 10] cents. Make 12 cents.

2
Greedy: 10¢ + 1¢ + 1¢ = 3 coins.
3
Optimal: 6¢ + 6¢ = 2 coins.
⚠
Greedy fails when denominations don't have the "canonical" property.

Nearest-neighbor algorithm (the Parcel Service pick)

def nearest_neighbor(start, points, distance_matrix):
 """Greedy TSP heuristic."""
 current = start
 unvisited = set(points)
 unvisited.remove(start)
 route = [start]
 total_distance = 0

 while unvisited:
 nearest = min(unvisited,
 key=lambda p: distance_matrix[current][p])
 total_distance += distance_matrix[current][nearest]
 route.append(nearest)
 current = nearest
 unvisited.remove(nearest)

 return route, total_distance
COMPLEXITY
Outer loop: n iterations.
Inner min(): O(n) scan of unvisited.
Total: O(n²).

Why nearest-neighbor isn't optimal

THE GREEDY TRAP
Picking the nearest neighbor RIGHT NOW can leave you stranded near distant unvisited points later.

Example: 4 cities in a line at 0, 1, 100, 102. Start at 1.
  Greedy: 1 → 0 → 100 → 102. Total = 1 + 100 + 2 = 103.
  Optimal: 1 → 100 → 102 → 0 = 99 + 2 + 102 = 203 ⚠ worse!
  Or: 0 → 1 → 100 → 102 = 1 + 99 + 2 = 102 (best).

Even this trivial example shows greedy can be far from optimal — but it's STILL useful because it's fast and "good enough."

Greedy approximation bounds

APPROXIMATION RATIO
Nearest-neighbor TSP: at MOST ~25 log n times optimal in the worst case.
In PRACTICE: typically 10-30% over optimal.

For the Parcel Service PA: NN at 130 miles vs optimal at ~110 miles. Both are well under 140-mile constraint, so NN passes.

Improving greedy: 2-opt swap

If your greedy route is too long, a simple post-processing step can improve it:

def two_opt(route, distance_matrix):
 """Try swapping pairs of edges; keep if shorter."""
 improved = True
 while improved:
 improved = False
 for i in range(1, len(route) - 1):
 for j in range(i + 1, len(route)):
 # Swap: reverse the segment between i and j
 new_route = route[:i] + route[i:j+1][::-1] + route[j+1:]
 if route_distance(new_route, distance_matrix) < route_distance(route, distance_matrix):
 route = new_route
 improved = True
 break
 return route
2-OPT
Repeatedly try reversing segments of the route.
Keep the change if it shortens the route.
Stop when no improvement is possible.

Complexity: O(n²) per pass; multiple passes possible.
Improvement: typically reduces NN route by 5-15%.

Why use greedy for Parcel Service instead of optimal TSP?

SECTION D LANGUAGE TEMPLATE
"I selected the GREEDY NEAREST-NEIGHBOR algorithm because:

  1. TSP is NP-hard. Brute-force enumeration is O(n!) — for 16 packages per truck, 16! = 2 × 10¹³ permutations, infeasible.
  2. NN runs in O(n²), completing routing for all trucks in microseconds.
  3. Result quality is sufficient. NN typically yields routes within 25% of optimal — well under the 140-mile constraint.
  4. Implementation simplicity: fewer lines of code, fewer bugs, easier to verify correctness.
  5. Defendable: standard, well-known algorithm with established literature.

Trade-off acknowledged: NN can produce up to 25-30% over optimal in adversarial cases. For Parcel Service, this is acceptable; for higher-stakes routing (e.g., commercial logistics), I would use 2-opt or simulated annealing as a refinement."

The greedy choice property — why it sometimes works

PROOF TECHNIQUE — EXCHANGE ARGUMENT
To prove greedy is optimal:
  1. Assume an optimal solution exists.
  2. Show that swapping the optimal's first decision for the greedy's choice doesn't make the solution worse.
  3. By induction, the all-greedy solution is also optimal.

This works for activity selection, MST, etc. — but FAILS for TSP, knapsack, and similar problems.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Assuming greedy = optimal. For TSP, knapsack, graph coloring, etc., it's NOT.

Forgetting that nearest-neighbor depends on the START point. Different starts → different routes.

Comparing greedy results across runs without controlling for start position.

Not mentioning the trade-off in your PA write-up — Section D wants strengths AND weaknesses.

Calling Dijkstra's "a heuristic" — it's PROVABLY OPTIMAL on graphs with non-negative weights.

★ ON THE PA AND OA

"What's the greedy choice for nearest-neighbor TSP?" → visit the closest unvisited city.

"Is greedy always optimal?" → NO. It's optimal for some problems (Dijkstra, MST) and a heuristic for others (TSP).

"Why use NN for Parcel Service instead of brute force?" → brute force is O(n!), NN is O(n²).

"Greedy fails when..." → no greedy choice property; locally optimal ≠ globally optimal.

"How to improve a greedy solution?" → 2-opt, simulated annealing, genetic algorithms.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Greedy = locally optimal choice, no backtracking
  • OPTIMAL for: Dijkstra, Kruskal/Prim MST, Huffman, activity selection
  • HEURISTIC for: TSP (nearest-neighbor), bin packing, graph coloring
  • Nearest-neighbor TSP: O(n²), typically within 25% of optimal
  • NN can be improved by 2-opt swap (5-15% reduction)
  • For Parcel Service PA: NN is the standard pick — fast, simple, defensible
  • Greedy choice property + optimal substructure → provably optimal
  • Discuss BOTH strengths and limitations in Section D
🧠 MEMORY AID

Greedy = grab the best-looking choice NOW and never look back. It is optimal only when the problem has the greedy-choice property plus optimal substructure (Dijkstra, Prim/Kruskal, Huffman). When a locally-best choice can block the global optimum (e.g., 0/1 knapsack), use dynamic programming instead.

★ ON THE OA / PA — WATCH FOR

A greedy algorithm makes the locally optimal choice each step, hoping for a global optimum. It works for MST (Prim/Kruskal), Dijkstra, Huffman, but FAILS for 0/1 knapsack and (generally) TSP. OA: identify when greedy is/ isn't optimal.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
coin change greedy (US coins) for 30c:
25 + 5 = 2 coins  (optimal here)

Result: greedy optimal only for some problems

Greedy is optimal only when the problem has the greedy-choice property; the OA tests recognizing problems where it breaks (e.g., 0/1 knapsack).

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Dynamic programming (DP) solves problems with OVERLAPPING subproblems by caching results — turning exponential algorithms into polynomial ones. Knapsack, longest common subsequence, edit distance, and matrix-chain multiplication all yield to DP. Even though Parcel Service doesn't directly use DP, the OA-style multiple choice questions on these problems show up frequently and you should be able to recognize and apply both flavors (memoization and tabulation).

The two prerequisites for DP

DP IS APPLICABLE WHEN
Optimal substructure: optimal solution can be built from optimal subsolutions.
Overlapping subproblems: the same subproblem is solved many times in a naive recursion.

Without OVERLAPPING subproblems, DP just becomes divide-and-conquer.
Without OPTIMAL SUBSTRUCTURE, you can't decompose at all.

Two flavors of DP

MEMOIZATION (TOP-DOWN)
Write the natural recursion.
Add a cache that maps "subproblem inputs" → "computed result."
Before computing, check cache; on return, store in cache.

Pros: matches problem structure naturally; only solves needed subproblems.
Cons: recursive overhead, deep call stacks.
TABULATION (BOTTOM-UP)
Build a TABLE of subproblem solutions, smallest first.
Each entry filled using values already computed.
Final answer is read off the table.

Pros: no recursion overhead, often more space-efficient.
Cons: may compute unneeded subproblems; less intuitive.

Fibonacci — the canonical DP intro

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Three Fibonacci implementations
# 1. Naive recursion: O(2^n) time, O(n) stack
def fib_naive(n):
 if n < 2: return n
 return fib_naive(n-1) + fib_naive(n-2)

# 2. Memoization (top-down): O(n) time, O(n) space
def fib_memo(n, cache={}):
 if n in cache: return cache[n]
 if n < 2: return n
 cache[n] = fib_memo(n-1) + fib_memo(n-2)
 return cache[n]

# 3. Tabulation (bottom-up): O(n) time, O(n) space
def fib_tab(n):
 if n < 2: return n
 table = [0] * (n + 1)
 table[1] = 1
 for i in range(2, n + 1):
 table[i] = table[i-1] + table[i-2]
 return table[n]

# 4. Tabulation with O(1) space
def fib_optimal(n):
 a, b = 0, 1
 for _ in range(n):
 a, b = b, a + b
 return a
1
Naive: 2^n calls — disastrous for n > 30.

0/1 Knapsack — classic DP

Problem: items with weights and values; pick a subset maximizing value subject to total weight ≤ W.

def knapsack(weights, values, W):
 """0/1 knapsack via tabulation. O(n*W) time and space."""
 n = len(weights)
 # dp[i][w] = max value using first i items with weight ≤ w
 dp = [[0] * (W + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]

 for i in range(1, n + 1):
 for w in range(W + 1):
 # Option A: skip item i
 best = dp[i-1][w]
 # Option B: take item i (if it fits)
 if weights[i-1] <= w:
 best = max(best, dp[i-1][w - weights[i-1]] + values[i-1])
 dp[i][w] = best

 return dp[n][W]
KNAPSACK ANALYSIS
Time: O(n × W) — fills an (n+1) × (W+1) table.
Space: O(n × W) — same table.
Pseudo-polynomial: polynomial in n × W, but W is exponential in input size (number of bits).
NP-hard in general, but tractable when W is small.

Longest Common Subsequence (LCS)

Problem: longest sequence appearing as a subsequence in both input strings.

def lcs(s1, s2):
 """LCS via tabulation. O(m*n) time and space."""
 m, n = len(s1), len(s2)
 dp = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]
 for i in range(1, m + 1):
 for j in range(1, n + 1):
 if s1[i-1] == s2[j-1]:
 dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1
 else:
 dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
 return dp[m][n]
LCS APPLICATIONS
Text diff (Git, Unix diff): finds matching lines.
DNA sequence alignment: matches base pairs.
File comparison: finds preserved sections across versions.

Edit Distance (Levenshtein)

Problem: minimum number of insertions, deletions, or substitutions to transform one string into another.

def edit_distance(s1, s2):
 m, n = len(s1), len(s2)
 dp = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]
 for i in range(m + 1): dp[i][0] = i # delete all
 for j in range(n + 1): dp[0][j] = j # insert all
 for i in range(1, m + 1):
 for j in range(1, n + 1):
 if s1[i-1] == s2[j-1]:
 dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]
 else:
 dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i-1][j], # delete
 dp[i][j-1], # insert
 dp[i-1][j-1]) # substitute
 return dp[m][n]
EDIT DISTANCE APPLICATIONS
Spell checkers — suggest corrections by smallest edit distance.
Autocomplete and fuzzy search.
DNA mutation analysis.
OCR error correction.

Steps to apply DP to a new problem

DP DESIGN PATTERN
1. Identify the subproblem: what does dp[i][j] represent?
2. Find the recurrence: how does dp[i][j] relate to smaller subproblems?
3. Identify base cases: where does the recursion bottom out?
4. Choose iteration order: smallest-to-largest along all dimensions.
5. Read the answer: which dp[i][j] contains the final result?
6. Optional: optimize space (e.g., keep only last row).

DP vs greedy vs divide-and-conquer

StrategySubproblemsDecisionOptimality
GreedyNo revisitLocal optimumSometimes
DPOverlappingTry all, cacheYes (when applicable)
Divide-conquerIndependentCombine subresultsYes

When NOT to use DP

DP IS OVERKILL WHEN
Subproblems don't overlap → use divide-and-conquer.
No optimal substructure → use brute force or heuristic.
Problem size is small → just enumerate.
Greedy works → it's faster (no table to fill).
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Mutable default arguments in Python (def f(n, cache={}):) — cache persists across calls. Use cache=None; if cache is None: cache = {}.

Wrong iteration order — fill smaller subproblems FIRST.

Wrong base cases — silently produce wrong answer.

Confusing memoization with caching at the wrong level — cache the FUNCTION RESULT, not intermediate variables.

Using DP when greedy works — wastes time and code.

★ ON THE OA

"DP requires what two properties?" → optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems.

"Memoization vs tabulation?" → top-down (recursion + cache) vs bottom-up (table).

"Knapsack complexity?" → O(n × W).

"Why is naive Fibonacci O(2^n)?" → branches into 2 each call.

"Why is memoized Fibonacci O(n)?" → each subproblem solved exactly once.

"Edit distance time?" → O(m × n).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • DP applies when: optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems
  • Memoization (top-down) = recursion + cache
  • Tabulation (bottom-up) = iterative table fill
  • Fibonacci: O(2^n) → O(n) via memoization → O(1) space iteratively
  • 0/1 Knapsack: O(n × W) DP solution
  • LCS, edit distance: O(m × n) DP solutions
  • DP design: identify subproblem → recurrence → base cases → iteration order → read answer
  • NOT for non-overlapping subproblems (use divide-and-conquer)
★ ON THE OA / PA — WATCH FOR

Dynamic programming solves overlapping subproblems once and stores results (memoization top-down / tabulation bottom-up). Turns exponential recursion into polynomial. OA: recognize DP problems (Fibonacci, knapsack, LCS) and the memo idea.

-> each value computed once -> O(n)

Result: memo turns O(2ⁿ) into O(n)

DP applies when subproblems overlap and have optimal substructure; caching results removes the repeated work that makes naive recursion exponential.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Divide-and-conquer is one of the most fundamental algorithm strategies. Merge sort, quicksort, binary search, FFT, and matrix multiplication all use it. The OA tests you on recognizing the strategy and analyzing its recurrences via the Master Theorem. This is also the conceptual basis for many parallel algorithms — divide work, conquer in parallel, combine results.

The three steps

DIVIDE-AND-CONQUER PATTERN
1. DIVIDE: split the problem into smaller subproblems of the SAME TYPE.
2. CONQUER: solve each subproblem (recursively if not trivial).
3. COMBINE: merge subproblem solutions into a solution for the original problem.

Most divide-and-conquer algorithms split into TWO subproblems of HALF size.

Binary search — minimal divide-and-conquer

def binary_search(arr, target, lo, hi):
 """Recursively search a sorted array."""
 if lo > hi: return -1 # base case: empty range
 mid = (lo + hi) // 2 # DIVIDE: pick middle
 if arr[mid] == target: return mid # CONQUER trivially
 if arr[mid] < target:
 return binary_search(arr, target, mid + 1, hi) # recurse right
 return binary_search(arr, target, lo, mid - 1) # recurse left
 # COMBINE step is trivial: just propagate the result
BINARY SEARCH ANALYSIS
Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1).
By Master Theorem: O(log n) time.
Space: O(log n) recursive (stack); O(1) iterative.

Merge sort — classic divide-and-conquer

def merge_sort(arr):
 """O(n log n) sort via divide-and-conquer."""
 if len(arr) <= 1: return arr
 mid = len(arr) // 2

 # DIVIDE
 left = arr[:mid]
 right = arr[mid:]

 # CONQUER (recurse on each half)
 left = merge_sort(left)
 right = merge_sort(right)

 # COMBINE (the merge step)
 return merge(left, right)

def merge(left, right):
 """Combine two sorted lists into one sorted list. O(n)."""
 result = []
 i = j = 0
 while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
 if left[i] <= right[j]:
 result.append(left[i]); i += 1
 else:
 result.append(right[j]); j += 1
 result.extend(left[i:])
 result.extend(right[j:])
 return result
MERGE SORT ANALYSIS
Recurrence: T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + O(n).
By Master Theorem (case 2): O(n log n) time.
Space: O(n) — the merge step requires temp storage.
Stable, deterministic, predictable. Used in Python's sorted() as part of Timsort.

Quicksort — divide-and-conquer with partitioning

def quicksort(arr, lo, hi):
 if lo < hi:
 # DIVIDE via partitioning
 pivot_index = partition(arr, lo, hi)
 # CONQUER both sides
 quicksort(arr, lo, pivot_index - 1)
 quicksort(arr, pivot_index + 1, hi)
 # COMBINE is trivial — array sorted in place

def partition(arr, lo, hi):
 pivot = arr[hi]
 i = lo - 1
 for j in range(lo, hi):
 if arr[j] <= pivot:
 i += 1
 arr[i], arr[j] = arr[j], arr[i]
 arr[i+1], arr[hi] = arr[hi], arr[i+1]
 return i + 1
QUICKSORT ANALYSIS
Best/Average: T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n log n).
Worst: pivot always at extreme (already-sorted input + naive pivot) → T(n) = T(n−1) + O(n) → O(n²).

In practice: faster than merge sort for in-memory arrays (better cache performance).
Used by Python's older sort, Java for primitive types.

The Master Theorem

MASTER THEOREM
For T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n) with a ≥ 1, b > 1:
Compare f(n) to n^(log_b a):
  Case 1: f(n) = O(n^(log_b a − ε)) → T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a))
  Case 2: f(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a)) → T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) · log n)
  Case 3: f(n) = Ω(n^(log_b a + ε)) → T(n) = Θ(f(n))

In English: compare the work done at the top to the leaves' work; the bigger one wins (or they tie, getting an extra log factor).
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Master Theorem applications
AlgorithmRecurrenceResult
Binary searchT(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)O(log n)
Merge sortT(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)O(n log n)
Naive matrix multT(n) = 8T(n/2) + O(n²)O(n³)
Strassen's matrixT(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n²)O(n^2.81)
Tree DFST(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1)O(n)

Other divide-and-conquer algorithms

CLASSIC EXAMPLES
Closest pair of points: O(n log n) — divide plane in half, find closest in each, then check the strip near the divider.
Karatsuba multiplication: O(n^1.585) — multiply n-digit numbers faster than schoolbook O(n²).
FFT (Fast Fourier Transform): O(n log n) — compute polynomial multiplication / spectrum analysis.
Strassen's matrix multiplication: O(n^2.81) — beats schoolbook O(n³) for large matrices.
Quickselect: O(n) average — find k-th smallest element without fully sorting.

Why divide-and-conquer is so powerful

THE LOG FACTOR APPEARS
Halving the problem at each step → recursion depth = log n.

This log factor is what makes O(n log n) sorts beat O(n²) sorts dramatically:
  n = 1M: O(n²) = 10¹² ops; O(n log n) = 2 × 10⁷ ops. 50,000× faster.
  n = 10M: O(n²) = 10¹⁴; O(n log n) = 2.3 × 10⁸. ~430,000× faster.

Most "fast" algorithms achieve their speed by getting that log factor.

Divide-and-conquer vs DP vs greedy

StrategySubproblem relationWhen to use
Divide-and-conquerIndependent (no overlap)Sort, search, FFT
DPOverlappingOptimization with overlap
GreedyNo revisitWhen greedy choice property holds

Parallel potential

Divide-and-conquer is naturally parallelizable: subproblems are independent, so they can be computed concurrently. Merge sort with k cores becomes O((n log n) / k) for the divide phase, with the merge step still O(n).

⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Confusing divide-and-conquer with DP — the difference is whether subproblems OVERLAP.

Quicksort worst case is O(n²) — happens with poor pivot choice on already-sorted input.

Forgetting Master Theorem only handles T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n) form.

Counting subproblem WORK twice — Master Theorem handles the recursion automatically.

Implementing merge sort recursively without enough temp space — needs O(n) extra.

★ ON THE OA

"What are the 3 steps of divide-and-conquer?" → divide, conquer, combine.

"Merge sort time complexity?" → O(n log n) all cases.

"Quicksort worst case?" → O(n²) — poor pivot, sorted input.

"Binary search recurrence?" → T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) → O(log n).

"Why is divide-and-conquer fast?" → splitting → log factor in recursion depth.

"State Master Theorem" → 3 cases comparing f(n) to n^(log_b a).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Pattern: Divide → Conquer → Combine
  • Subproblems are INDEPENDENT (no overlap — that's DP)
  • Recursion depth = O(log n); the log factor is the secret to speed
  • Binary search: O(log n); merge sort / quicksort avg: O(n log n)
  • Quicksort worst case: O(n²) on adversarial input
  • Master Theorem: solves T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n) recurrences
  • Famous algorithms: closest-pair O(n log n), FFT O(n log n), Strassen O(n^2.81)
  • Naturally parallelizable — independent subproblems
★ ON THE OA / PA — WATCH FOR

Divide & conquer: split, solve recursively, combine. Examples: merge sort, quicksort, binary search. Analyzed with recurrences / the Master Theorem. Contrast with DP (D&C subproblems usually DON'T overlap).

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
merge sort: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)  ->  O(n log n)

Result: split-solve-combine → often n log n

D&C divides into independent subproblems; DP is for overlapping ones. The recurrence 2T(n/2)+n resolving to n log n is worth memorizing.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Backtracking and heuristics are how we attack NP-hard problems — those without efficient exact algorithms. Backtracking explores the solution space systematically, abandoning paths that can't succeed. Heuristics give "good enough" answers fast. Both are essential for the Parcel Service PA where TSP is NP-hard, and both appear on the OA as conceptual questions about algorithm strategies.

Backtracking — systematic search with pruning

BACKTRACKING TEMPLATE
1. Make a choice: extend the current partial solution.
2. Recurse: try to complete the solution from this state.
3. If solution complete: record it (or return success).
4. If dead end: undo the choice (backtrack) and try next option.
5. Pruning: skip choices that provably can't lead to a valid solution.

The N-Queens problem — classic backtracking

Problem: place n queens on an n × n chess board so no two attack each other.

def solve_nqueens(n):
 """Return all solutions to N-Queens."""
 solutions = []
 # board[i] = column of queen in row i
 board = [-1] * n
 backtrack(board, 0, n, solutions)
 return solutions

def backtrack(board, row, n, solutions):
 if row == n:
 solutions.append(board[:]) # complete solution found
 return
 for col in range(n):
 if is_safe(board, row, col):
 board[row] = col # MAKE CHOICE
 backtrack(board, row + 1, n, solutions) # RECURSE
 board[row] = -1 # UNDO CHOICE (backtrack)

def is_safe(board, row, col):
 """Check if placing a queen at (row, col) conflicts with previous rows."""
 for prev_row in range(row):
 prev_col = board[prev_row]
 if prev_col == col: return False # same column
 if abs(prev_col - col) == abs(prev_row - row): return False # diagonal
 return True
N-QUEENS COMPLEXITY
Without pruning: O(n^n) — try every queen in every column.
With backtracking pruning: roughly O(n!) — but in practice MUCH faster because most paths get pruned early.
Solvable for n up to ~25 via backtracking; beyond that, special techniques.

Other backtracking problems

CLASSIC BACKTRACKING APPLICATIONS
Sudoku: try a digit, recurse, undo if invalid.
Maze solving: try each direction, backtrack on dead ends.
Word search puzzles: try each letter direction.
Subset sum: try including or excluding each element.
Permutations and combinations: try each next element.
Graph coloring: try each color for each vertex.
Crossword puzzles: try each candidate word for each slot.

Branch and bound — backtracking with optimization

BRANCH AND BOUND
Backtracking + an UPPER BOUND on the best possible solution from the current branch.
If the bound is worse than the best solution found so far, PRUNE the branch.

Used for OPTIMIZATION problems (find best solution, not just any).
Example: branch-and-bound TSP — track shortest tour found so far; prune any branch whose lower-bound exceeds it.

Heuristics — sacrifice optimality for speed

HEURISTIC
An approximation algorithm that:
  Runs in polynomial (often O(n²) or better) time.
  Produces a solution that's "good enough" for the use case.
  May be far from optimal in adversarial cases.

Used when exact solutions are too slow (NP-hard problems).

Common heuristics for NP-hard problems

ProblemHeuristicQuality
TSPNearest-neighbor~25% over optimal
TSP2-opt local search~5% over optimal
TSP (metric)Christofides≤ 1.5× optimal (proven)
Bin packingFirst-fit decreasing≤ 11/9 × optimal
KnapsackGreedy by value/weight ratioNo bound (can be terrible)
Vertex coverGreedy≤ 2× optimal

Metaheuristics — generic optimization frameworks

METAHEURISTICS
Simulated annealing: random walk that accepts worse solutions with decreasing probability — escapes local minima.
Genetic algorithms: evolve a population of candidate solutions via mutation and crossover.
Tabu search: local search that remembers recently visited solutions to avoid cycles.
Ant colony optimization: simulate ants leaving pheromone trails on good paths.

All can be applied to TSP, scheduling, vehicle routing, etc.

Why nearest-neighbor for Parcel Service, not optimal?

SECTION D / F LANGUAGE
"Optimal TSP solutions for n cities require O(n!) time via brute force or O(n² · 2^n) via dynamic programming (Held-Karp). For 16 packages per truck, this is 2 × 10¹³ permutations or 1.7 × 10⁷ DP cells — feasible for DP, but with significant code complexity. Branch-and-bound could find optimal in reasonable time but with intricate pruning logic. Simulated annealing or genetic algorithms could approach optimal but require parameter tuning.

Nearest-neighbor at O(n²) yields a route well under the 140-mile constraint and is straightforward to implement and verify. The accuracy gap (typically 10-25%) is acceptable for this use case. For higher-precision routing, I would augment with 2-opt local search as a refinement pass."

Backtracking as a basis for heuristics

Backtracking explores ALL possibilities exhaustively (with pruning). Heuristics try ONE good guess. The middle ground — branch-and-bound or beam search — explores a few promising paths and prunes the rest.

SPECTRUM
Brute force ←→ Backtracking ←→ Branch-and-bound ←→ Heuristic ←→ Random guess
  (slow, optimal)                                                                                              (fast, terrible)

Pick the rightmost approach that gives "good enough" results.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Confusing backtracking with brute force — backtracking PRUNES; brute force tries everything.

Forgetting to UNDO the choice in backtracking — leads to wrong "complete solution" detection.

Using backtracking when DP would work — wastes time on overlapping subproblems.

Calling NN a "guarantee" — it's a heuristic, not provably optimal.

Implementing simulated annealing without temperature scheduling — degenerates to random walk.

★ ON THE OA

"What's backtracking?" → systematic exploration with undo on dead ends.

"Classic backtracking problems?" → N-Queens, Sudoku, maze, subset sum.

"Heuristic vs exact algorithm?" → heuristic: fast, possibly suboptimal. Exact: slow, guaranteed optimal.

"Why use heuristics for TSP?" → TSP is NP-hard; exact would be too slow for moderate n.

"Examples of heuristics?" → nearest-neighbor, 2-opt, Christofides, simulated annealing.

"Branch-and-bound vs backtracking?" → adds an upper-bound prune for optimization problems.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Backtracking: systematic search; make choice → recurse → UNDO on dead end
  • Classic problems: N-Queens, Sudoku, maze, subset sum
  • Branch and bound: backtracking + upper bound for pruning
  • Heuristic: fast, possibly suboptimal — used when exact is too slow
  • NN TSP: ~25% over optimal; 2-opt: ~5% over; Christofides: ≤ 1.5× (proven)
  • Metaheuristics: simulated annealing, GA, tabu search, ant colony
  • For Parcel Service PA: NN is the right pick — fast, simple, sufficient
  • NEVER guess: the rubric wants a JUSTIFICATION (Section D)
★ ON THE OA / PA — WATCH FOR

Backtracking explores choices and undoes them on failure (N-queens, maze, subsets) — exponential worst case but prunes. Heuristics trade optimality for speed on hard problems (e.g., nearest-neighbor for TSP, used in the PA).

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
nearest-neighbor TSP: from current stop,
  always go to the closest unvisited stop

Result: heuristic gives a good, not optimal, route

The PA's routing uses a nearest-neighbor heuristic — fast and 'good enough', not guaranteed optimal. Know why exact TSP is infeasible at scale.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

BSTs are the workhorse of ordered data — anywhere you need fast insert, lookup, AND sorted traversal. The OA tests insert/delete operations and recognizing degenerate cases. More importantly, this section motivates WHY we need self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) — without balancing, a BST can degenerate into a linked list.

The BST property

BST INVARIANT
For every node N:
  Every key in the LEFT subtree of N is < N.key
  Every key in the RIGHT subtree of N is > N.key

This must hold RECURSIVELY — not just for direct children.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Valid vs invalid BST
 8 8
 / \ / \
 3 10 3 10
 / \ \ / \ \
 1 6 14 1 6 14
 / \ /
 4 7 12
 
 VALID BST INVALID! 12 is in 14's left
 subtree but 12 < 8 should be on 8's left

The BST property must hold ALL THE WAY UP, not just compared to the immediate parent.

BST operations

Search

def search(node, key):
 if node is None:
 return None
 if key == node.key:
 return node
 if key < node.key:
 return search(node.left, key)
 return search(node.right, key)

Time: O(h) where h = height. For balanced BST: O(log n). Worst case: O(n).

Insert

def insert(node, key):
 if node is None:
 return Node(key)
 if key < node.key:
 node.left = insert(node.left, key)
 elif key > node.key:
 node.right = insert(node.right, key)
 # Equal keys ignored (or could handle as duplicates)
 return node

Delete (3 cases)

def delete(node, key):
 if node is None: return None
 if key < node.key:
 node.left = delete(node.left, key)
 elif key > node.key:
 node.right = delete(node.right, key)
 else: # found the node
 # Case 1: no children — just remove
 if node.left is None and node.right is None:
 return None
 # Case 2: one child — replace with that child
 if node.left is None: return node.right
 if node.right is None: return node.left
 # Case 3: two children — replace with in-order successor
 successor = min_node(node.right)
 node.key = successor.key
 node.right = delete(node.right, successor.key)
 return node

def min_node(node):
 while node.left is not None:
 node = node.left
 return node
DELETION CASES
Case 1: leaf — just remove it.
Case 2: one child — promote the child to the deleted node's position.
Case 3: two children — find IN-ORDER SUCCESSOR (smallest in right subtree), copy its key, then delete it from right subtree.

Alternative for case 3: use IN-ORDER PREDECESSOR (largest in left subtree).

Traversals (revisited)

TraversalOrderOutput for BST
In-orderL → Node → RSorted ascending
Pre-orderNode → L → RUseful for tree copy
Post-orderL → R → NodeUseful for tree deletion
Reverse in-orderR → Node → LSorted descending

The killer feature: in-order traversal of a BST yields all keys in SORTED ORDER, in O(n) time, with no actual sorting effort. This is why BSTs exist as a separate structure rather than just "an ordered hash table."

BST height — the critical metric

HEIGHT-DEPENDENT COMPLEXITY
All BST operations take O(h) where h is the tree's height.

Best case (perfectly balanced): h = ⌊log₂ n⌋ → O(log n) operations.
Worst case (degenerate / skewed): h = n - 1 → O(n) operations.

This is why balance MATTERS so much.

Degenerate BST cases

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Inserting sorted keys gives a linked list

Insert keys 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 into an empty BST IN ORDER.

1
Insert 1: root.
2
Insert 2: goes right of 1.
3
Insert 3: goes right of 2.
⚠
After all 5 inserts, the tree is a chain: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 (right children only).
5
Search for 5 takes 5 comparisons — O(n), not O(log n).
✓
Same data inserted in random order would give h ≈ log₂(5) ≈ 2-3.

What causes degeneration?

DEGENERATION TRIGGERS
Inserting in sorted order: each insert goes only one direction.
Inserting in reverse-sorted order: same, but skewed left.
Adversarial inputs: if attacker controls input, they can force worst-case.
Real-world data (e.g., timestamps): often arrives sorted.

Random insertions usually give O(log n) average height — but real systems can't rely on randomness.

The need for self-balancing trees

WHY AVL AND RED-BLACK EXIST
Standard BSTs DON'T self-balance — they trust the insertion order.

Self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black, splay, B-trees) maintain O(log n) height automatically by performing ROTATIONS during insert/delete.

Cost: slightly slower constant factors per operation.
Benefit: GUARANTEED O(log n) — no degenerate cases.

Used in: Java TreeMap (red-black), C++ std::map (red-black), database indices (B-trees).

BST vs hash table

PropertyBST (balanced)Hash table
Insert / Lookup / DeleteO(log n)O(1) average
Sorted iterationO(n) — yesNo
Range queries (e.g. "all keys 5-10")O(log n + k)O(n) — must scan all
Min / maxO(log n)O(n)
Memory overhead2 pointers per nodeSparse buckets + chains

For the Parcel Service PA, hash table beats BST because there's no need for ordered iteration — random access by ID is what's needed.

BST applications

WHERE BSTs APPEAR
Database indices (especially B-trees, generalized BSTs)
Java TreeMap, TreeSet (red-black BST under the hood)
C++ std::map, std::set (red-black BST)
Symbol tables in compilers
Auto-complete (sometimes via tries, but BSTs work)
Order statistics (k-th smallest)
Maintaining a sorted "live" data set
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

BST property is RECURSIVE — every key in left subtree must be less than the ROOT, not just the immediate parent.

Forgetting deletion case 3 (two children) — must use in-order successor or predecessor.

Trusting that BST gives O(log n) — only TRUE for balanced trees.

Inserting sorted data → degenerate to linked list.

Treating in-order, pre-order, post-order as interchangeable — they give different traversal orders.

★ ON THE OA

"What's the BST property?" → left subtree all < root; right subtree all > root; recursively.

"In-order traversal of BST yields?" → sorted ascending order.

"BST insert/lookup complexity?" → O(h) where h is height; O(log n) balanced, O(n) worst.

"What causes BST degeneration?" → inserting sorted data with no balancing.

"BST delete case with 2 children?" → replace with in-order successor (or predecessor).

"Why need self-balancing trees?" → guarantee O(log n) regardless of insert order.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • BST property: left < node < right (RECURSIVELY)
  • All operations O(h) — height matters
  • Balanced: O(log n). Degenerate: O(n).
  • In-order traversal of BST = sorted output
  • Delete cases: leaf, one child, two children (use in-order successor)
  • Inserting sorted data → linked list (worst case)
  • Self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) fix this automatically
  • For Parcel Service: hash table beats BST (no ordered iteration needed)
★ ON THE OA / PA — WATCH FOR

BST ops are O(h); balanced h≈log n, degenerate h=n. This motivates SELF-BALANCING trees. OA: why a plain BST can degrade to O(n) (sorted inserts) and how balancing fixes it.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
insert 1,2,3,4 into a plain BST
-> right-leaning chain, height 3 -> O(n) ops

Result: sorted inserts → degenerate O(n) BST

A plain BST offers no balance guarantee, so adversarial (sorted) input makes it a linked list; AVL/red-black trees restore O(log n).

TermDefinition

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

AVL trees are the OG self-balancing BST — invented in 1962, still the standard textbook example. They guarantee O(log n) operations by tracking each node's "balance factor" and performing ROTATIONS when it goes out of bounds. The OA tests rotation cases (LL, RR, LR, RL) directly. Knowing them cold is half the AVL battle.

What "AVL" means

AVL TREE INVARIANT
Named after inventors Adelson-Velsky and Landis (1962).

For EVERY node N: |height(N.left) − height(N.right)| ≤ 1.

In English: the heights of left and right subtrees differ by at most 1.

This guarantees tree height = O(log n).

Balance factor

BALANCE FACTOR DEFINITION
balance_factor(N) = height(N.left) - height(N.right)

Possible values for an AVL-valid node: -1, 0, +1.
ANY OTHER VALUE means the tree needs rebalancing.

Convention: height of an empty tree (None) is -1; height of a single node is 0.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Compute balance factors
 30 Node 30: height(left=2) - height(right=1) = +1 ✓
 / \ Node 20: height(left=0) - height(right=1) = -1 ✓
 20 40 Node 10: height(left=-1) - height(right=-1) = 0 ✓
 / \ \ Node 25: leaf → 0 ✓
 10 25 45 Node 40: 0
 Node 45: 0

All factors in {-1, 0, +1} → tree is AVL-valid.

The four rotation cases

WHEN ROTATIONS HAPPEN
After insert or delete, walk back UP the tree from the modified node.
At each ancestor, recompute height and balance factor.
If factor becomes +2 or -2, perform the appropriate rotation.

Four cases based on WHERE the imbalance came from:
CaseInsertion sideRotation
LLLeft of left childSingle right rotation
RRRight of right childSingle left rotation
LRRight of left childLeft, then right (double)
RLLeft of right childRight, then left (double)

Single right rotation (LL case)

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Insert 1, 2, 3 sequentially
After inserting 3, 2, 1:

 / / \
 2 ROTATE RIGHT 1 3
 / ─────────────►
 1
 
Balance factor at 3 was +2 (left-heavy) AVL again
Subtree was LEFT-LEFT heavy
1
3 has left child 2; 2 has left child 1. Imbalance is on LEFT-LEFT side.
📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
2
Rotate right at 3: 2 becomes the new root, 3 becomes its right child.
✓
Tree balanced. All balance factors back in {-1, 0, +1}.

Single left rotation (RR case)

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Insert 1, 2, 3 (mirror of above)
After inserting 1, 2, 3:
 1 2
 \ / \
 2 ROTATE LEFT 1 3
 \ ────────────►

Balance factor at 1 was -2 (right-heavy) AVL again
Subtree was RIGHT-RIGHT heavy

Double rotation: left-then-right (LR case)

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Insert 3, 1, 2
After inserting 3, 1, 2:
 3 3 2
 / / / \
 1 LEFT 2 RIGHT 1 3
 \ ROTATE / ROTATE
 2 (at 1) 1 (at 3)
 
3 is left-heavy with right-heavy left child = LEFT-RIGHT case
Need: left rotate at 1 first, THEN right rotate at 3
1
Imbalance shape: left subtree has a right child sticking out (a "zigzag").
2
First, left-rotate the LEFT CHILD (1) — converts to LL case.
3
Then, right-rotate at the imbalanced node (3) — fixes the LL.
✓
Tree balanced.

Double rotation: right-then-left (RL case)

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Insert 1, 3, 2
After inserting 1, 3, 2:
 1 1 2
 \ \ / \
 3 RIGHT 2 LEFT 1 3
 / ROTATE \ ROTATE
 2 (at 3) 3 (at 1)
 
1 is right-heavy with left-heavy right child = RIGHT-LEFT case
Need: right rotate at 3 first, THEN left rotate at 1

How to identify which rotation case

DECISION TREE
At the imbalanced node N (factor = ±2):

IF balance_factor(N) == +2 (LEFT-heavy):
  IF balance_factor(N.left) ≥ 0 → LL case → single RIGHT rotate at N
  ELSE → LR case → left rotate at N.left, then right rotate at N

IF balance_factor(N) == -2 (RIGHT-heavy):
  IF balance_factor(N.right) ≤ 0 → RR case → single LEFT rotate at N
  ELSE → RL case → right rotate at N.right, then left rotate at N

Right rotation primitive (the building block)

def rotate_right(y):
 """
 Rotate right at node y.
 Before: y After: x
 / \ / \
 x T3 T1 y
 / \ / \
 T1 T2 T2 T3
 """
 x = y.left
 T2 = x.right

 x.right = y
 y.left = T2

 # Update heights (compute from children)
 y.height = 1 + max(height(y.left), height(y.right))
 x.height = 1 + max(height(x.left), height(x.right))

 return x # new root of this subtree

Left rotation primitive

def rotate_left(x):
 """
 Rotate left at node x.
 Before: x After: y
 / \ / \
 T1 y x T3
 / \ / \
 T2 T3 T1 T2
 """
 y = x.right
 T2 = y.left

 y.left = x
 x.right = T2

 x.height = 1 + max(height(x.left), height(x.right))
 y.height = 1 + max(height(y.left), height(y.right))

 return y # new root of this subtree

Why rotations preserve BST property

Both rotations preserve the in-order traversal of the subtree. If you write out the in-order before and after a rotation, you get the same sequence — just reorganized into a tree of different shape. This is why rotations don't break the BST property.

PROOF SKETCH
Right rotation at y: in-order before = (T1, x, T2, y, T3) = in-order after = (T1, x, T2, y, T3). Same.
Left rotation at x: in-order before = (T1, x, T2, y, T3) = in-order after = (T1, x, T2, y, T3). Same.

Rotations are LOCAL transformations that preserve the global ordering.

Cost of rotation

ROTATION COMPLEXITY
Each rotation: O(1) — just a few pointer swaps and height updates.
After insert/delete, rotations may cascade UP the tree.
But: at most O(log n) rotations needed per insert/delete.

So insert and delete remain O(log n) total.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Confusing LL with LR — LL means imbalance was inserted on left-LEFT; LR means left-RIGHT (zigzag).

Right rotation moves the LEFT child UP (not right). Confusing direction.

Forgetting to update heights AFTER rotation.

Forgetting to return the new subtree root from the rotation function.

Computing balance_factor wrong direction: it's LEFT minus RIGHT, not the other way.

Treating an empty subtree as height 0 (it should be -1, so leaf height = 0).

★ ON THE OA

"What's an AVL tree?" → BST where |bf| ≤ 1 for every node.

"Balance factor formula?" → height(left) - height(right).

"Allowed BF values?" → {-1, 0, +1}.

"What rotation for LL imbalance?" → single right rotation.

"What rotation for RR?" → single left.

"LR rotation?" → left at child, then right at imbalanced node.

"AVL operation complexity?" → O(log n).

"How to identify the rotation case?" → check imbalanced node's BF, then its child's BF.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • AVL invariant: |bf| ≤ 1 at every node
  • Balance factor = height(left) − height(right)
  • Allowed values: -1, 0, +1; need rebalance at ±2
  • Four rotation cases: LL, RR (single); LR, RL (double)
  • LL → right rotate; RR → left rotate
  • LR → left at child then right at node; RL → right at child then left at node
  • Each rotation: O(1); total per insert/delete: O(log n)
  • Rotations preserve in-order traversal (BST property)
🧠 MEMORY AID

AVL balance factor = height(left) − height(right), and it must stay in {−1, 0, +1}. Four rotation cases: LL → right, RR → left, LR → left-then-right, RL → right-then-left. Straight line = single rotation; zig-zag = double rotation.

★ ON THE OA / PA — WATCH FOR

AVL balance factor = height(left) − height(right), must be −1, 0, or +1. Violations trigger rotations: LL→right, RR→left, LR→left-then-right, RL→right-then-left. OA: compute a balance factor or name the rotation.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
insert into left-left case -> single RIGHT rotation
BF of node becomes +2 -> rotate to restore

Result: |BF| ≤ 1; else rotate

The balance factor detects imbalance; the four rotation cases restore it. Being able to identify the case from the insertion path is core AVL content.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Knowing rotations is one thing — knowing WHEN to rotate during insert/delete operations is what makes AVL work. This section walks through full insert and delete with rebalancing logic and complexity. The OA tests this combination directly: "after inserting X into this AVL tree, what does it look like?"

AVL insert — full algorithm

def avl_insert(node, key):
 """Insert key into AVL tree rooted at node. Returns new root."""
 # 1. Standard BST insert
 if node is None:
 return Node(key)
 if key < node.key:
 node.left = avl_insert(node.left, key)
 elif key > node.key:
 node.right = avl_insert(node.right, key)
 else:
 return node # duplicate — ignore

 # 2. Update height of this ancestor
 node.height = 1 + max(height(node.left), height(node.right))

 # 3. Get balance factor
 bf = balance_factor(node)

 # 4. If unbalanced, perform rotations
 # LL case
 if bf > 1 and key < node.left.key:
 return rotate_right(node)
 # RR case
 if bf < -1 and key > node.right.key:
 return rotate_left(node)
 # LR case
 if bf > 1 and key > node.left.key:
 node.left = rotate_left(node.left)
 return rotate_right(node)
 # RL case
 if bf < -1 and key < node.right.key:
 node.right = rotate_right(node.right)
 return rotate_left(node)

 # 5. No rebalance needed
 return node

def balance_factor(node):
 if node is None: return 0
 return height(node.left) - height(node.right)

def height(node):
 if node is None: return -1
 return node.height

Full insert example

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Insert 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 25
Step 1-2: Insert 10, then 20:
 10
 \
 20 bf at 10 = -1, OK

Step 3: Insert 30 → bf at 10 = -2 (RR case)
 10 20
 \ / \

 \

Step 4: Insert 40:
 20
 / \

 \
 40 bf at 30 = -1, bf at 20 = -1, OK

Step 5: Insert 50 → bf at 30 = -2 (RR case at 30)
 20 20
 / \ / \
 10 30 → 10 40
 \ / \
 40 30 50
 \

Step 6: Insert 25:
 20
 / \
 10 40
 / \
 30 50
 /
 25 bf at 30 = +1, bf at 40 = +1, bf at 20 = -1, OK

AVL delete — more complex

def avl_delete(node, key):
 """Delete key from AVL tree. Returns new root."""
 if node is None: return node

 # 1. Standard BST delete
 if key < node.key:
 node.left = avl_delete(node.left, key)
 elif key > node.key:
 node.right = avl_delete(node.right, key)
 else:
 # Found the node — perform deletion (3 cases as before)
 if node.left is None:
 return node.right
 if node.right is None:
 return node.left
 # Two children: replace with in-order successor
 successor = min_node(node.right)
 node.key = successor.key
 node.right = avl_delete(node.right, successor.key)

 # 2. Update height
 node.height = 1 + max(height(node.left), height(node.right))

 # 3. Get balance factor
 bf = balance_factor(node)

 # 4. Rebalance if needed (4 cases)
 # LL: left-heavy and left child is left-heavy or balanced
 if bf > 1 and balance_factor(node.left) >= 0:
 return rotate_right(node)
 # LR: left-heavy and left child is right-heavy
 if bf > 1 and balance_factor(node.left) < 0:
 node.left = rotate_left(node.left)
 return rotate_right(node)
 # RR: right-heavy and right child is right-heavy or balanced
 if bf < -1 and balance_factor(node.right) <= 0:
 return rotate_left(node)
 # RL: right-heavy and right child is left-heavy
 if bf < -1 and balance_factor(node.right) > 0:
 node.right = rotate_right(node.right)
 return rotate_left(node)

 return node
DELETE NUANCE
Unlike insert, after delete the rotation case is determined by the BALANCE FACTOR of the child (not by the inserted key's position).

Insert: "I just inserted on the LEFT-LEFT side, do an LL rotation."
Delete: "After removal, the imbalance is shaped LEFT-LEFT-or-balanced, do an LL rotation."

Also: a single delete can trigger MULTIPLE rotations as you walk back up the tree.

Insert vs delete — rotation count

OperationMax rotations
InsertAt most 1 rotation (single or double)
DeleteUp to O(log n) rotations cascading up

Delete is the more expensive operation. Some applications (e.g., real-time systems) prefer red-black trees for slightly faster delete.

AVL operation complexity

OperationTimeSpace
SearchO(log n)O(log n) recursive
InsertO(log n)O(log n)
DeleteO(log n)O(log n)
In-order traversalO(n)O(log n)
Min / maxO(log n)O(log n)

Why "self-adjusting"?

SELF-ADJUSTING
AVL trees automatically restructure themselves to maintain balance.
No external "rebalance" call is needed.
This makes them a "self-adjusting" data structure — qualifying for the C950 PA Section C6 requirement.

Hash tables and AVL trees are both common examples of self-adjusting structures used in answers.

AVL vs other balanced trees

PropertyAVLRed-Black
Height bound≤ 1.44 log₂ n (tighter)≤ 2 log₂(n+1) (looser)
Lookup speedFaster (shorter trees)Slightly slower
Insert/delete speedMore rotations (slower)Fewer rotations (faster)
Best forRead-heavy workloadsMixed read/write
Used inMemory databasesJava TreeMap, C++ std::map
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Forgetting to update height AFTER recursing on insert/delete.

Mixing up rotation cases between insert (key-based) and delete (BF-based).

Not handling cascading rotations on delete — must recurse all the way to the root.

Treating AVL as "always faster than BST" — it has higher constant factors per insert/delete.

Using AVL when a hash table would do — overkill if no ordered iteration is needed.

★ ON THE OA

"AVL insert complexity?" → O(log n).

"AVL delete complexity?" → O(log n) but with up to log n rotations.

"After inserting X, what's the new tree?" → walk through BST insert, then check BFs, rotate.

"Why is AVL self-adjusting?" → automatic rebalancing via rotations.

"AVL vs red-black?" → AVL = stricter balance, slower writes; RB = looser, faster writes.

"In-order traversal of AVL?" → still sorted (rotations preserve in-order).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Red-black trees are the most commonly used self-balancing BST in production. Java's TreeMap, C++'s std::map, the Linux kernel's process scheduler, and many database indices all use them. They're slightly more relaxed than AVL trees — taller but with fewer rotations on insert/delete. The OA tests recognition of red-black properties and high-level comparison to AVL.

The five red-black properties

RED-BLACK INVARIANTS
1. Every node is either RED or BLACK.
2. The ROOT is BLACK.
3. Every LEAF (NIL/null) is BLACK.
4. If a node is RED, both children must be BLACK (no two red nodes in a row).
5. Every path from any node to its descendant leaves contains the SAME NUMBER of black nodes.

These five rules together guarantee tree height ≤ 2 · log₂(n + 1).

Why these properties keep the tree balanced

HEIGHT BOUND PROOF SKETCH
Property 4: red nodes can't be adjacent → at most half the path from root to leaf is red.
Property 5: every path has the same black-node count.

Therefore: longest path ≤ 2 × shortest path.
Combined with the standard BST height bound: red-black height = O(log n).

How balance is maintained

RED-BLACK MAINTENANCE
After insert/delete, the algorithm performs:
  Recoloring: change red ↔ black (no structural change).
  Rotations: same single/double rotations as AVL.

At most 2 rotations per insert; at most 3 per delete.
Recoloring may cascade up the tree but is O(log n).

Insert in red-black trees

INSERT ALGORITHM
1. Standard BST insert.
2. Color the new node RED (preserves property 5).
3. If parent is BLACK: done. Tree is still valid.
4. If parent is RED: violates property 4 ("red-red"). Fix via:
  Case A: uncle is RED → recolor parent + uncle BLACK, recolor grandparent RED, recurse on grandparent.
  Case B: uncle is BLACK → rotate (single or double) and recolor.
5. Final: root is colored BLACK.

Delete in red-black trees

Deletion is intricate — six cases depending on the deleted node's color and its sibling's color/children. The high-level idea:

DELETE OUTLINE
1. Standard BST delete.
2. If deleted node was RED: done (no property violated).
3. If deleted node was BLACK: violates property 5 (path now has fewer blacks).
4. Fix-up via 6 cases involving sibling color, sibling's children's colors, and rotation.

Net result: at most 3 rotations + O(log n) recoloring.

RULE OF THUMB
Reads dominate? → AVL.
Writes are frequent? → Red-Black.
Don't know? → Red-Black is the safer default.

For the Parcel Service PA, you'll represent the 27-address distance table as a graph. The choice between adjacency list and adjacency matrix affects both your code's complexity and your write-up's defensibility. Graph terminology refresher

CORE TERMS
Graph G = (V, E): set of vertices V and edges E.
Directed graph: edges have direction (one-way).
Undirected graph: edges are bidirectional.
Weighted graph: each edge has a numeric weight (distance, cost, capacity).
Sparse graph: |E| ≈ |V| (few edges per vertex).
Dense graph: |E| ≈ |V|² (most pairs connected).
Connected: every vertex reachable from every other.
DAG: directed acyclic graph (no cycles).

Adjacency matrix

ADJACENCY MATRIX
A V × V grid where M[i][j] holds the weight of edge from vertex i to j.
Use 0, infinity, or None to indicate "no edge."

Space: O(V²) regardless of edge count.
Edge query (i, j): O(1) — direct lookup.
Iterate neighbors of i: O(V) — must scan entire row.
Add edge: O(1).
Remove edge: O(1). 
class AdjacencyMatrix:
 def __init__(self, n):
 self.n = n
 # Initialize to infinity (no edge)
 INF = float('inf')
 self.matrix = [[INF] * n for _ in range(n)]
 # Diagonal = 0 (distance from vertex to itself)
 for i in range(n):
 self.matrix[i][i] = 0

 def add_edge(self, u, v, weight, directed=False):
 self.matrix[u][v] = weight
 if not directed:
 self.matrix[v][u] = weight

 def get_weight(self, u, v):
 return self.matrix[u][v]

 def neighbors(self, u):
 return [v for v in range(self.n)
 if v != u and self.matrix[u][v] != float('inf')]

Adjacency list

ADJACENCY LIST
An array (or hash table) where index/key i holds a list of (neighbor, weight) pairs.

Space: O(V + E) — proportional to actual edge count.
Edge query (i, j): O(deg(i)) — must scan i's list.
Iterate neighbors of i: O(deg(i)) — directly available.
Add edge: O(1) (append to list).
Remove edge: O(deg(i)) — must search. 
class AdjacencyList:
 def __init__(self):
 self.adj = {} # vertex -> list of (neighbor, weight)

 def add_vertex(self, u):
 if u not in self.adj:
 self.adj[u] = []

 def add_edge(self, u, v, weight, directed=False):
 self.add_vertex(u)
 self.add_vertex(v)
 self.adj[u].append((v, weight))
 if not directed:
 self.adj[v].append((u, weight))

 def get_weight(self, u, v):
 for neighbor, weight in self.adj.get(u, []):
 if neighbor == v:
 return weight
 return float('inf')

 def neighbors(self, u):
 return [neighbor for neighbor, _ in self.adj.get(u, [])]

Which to use when?

DECISION GUIDE
Dense graph (E ≈ V²): matrix wins — same space, faster edge lookup.
Sparse graph (E ≈ V): list wins — much less space, faster neighbor iteration.
Frequent edge weight queries: matrix.
Frequent neighbor iteration (BFS, DFS, Dijkstra): list.
Small graphs (V ≤ 1000): matrix is fine, simpler.
Large sparse graphs (V > 10,000): list is essential.

Parcel Service GRAPH CHOICE
V = 27 (addresses including hub).
Distance table is COMPLETE — every pair has a distance → DENSE.
Matrix space: 27² = 729 cells. Trivial.
Edge weight queries: O(1) via matrix lookup.

Use ADJACENCY MATRIX for the Parcel Service distance table. Simpler code, faster lookups, negligible memory. 
def load_distances(filename):
 """Read Parcel Service distance CSV into an adjacency matrix.
 Returns (matrix, address_to_index)."""
 address_to_index = {}
 rows = []
 with open(filename) as f:
 for line in f:
 cells = line.strip().split(',')
 address = cells[0]
 address_to_index[address] = len(rows)
 distances = [float(c) if c else 0.0 for c in cells[1:]]
 rows.append(distances)

 n = len(rows)
 # Mirror the lower triangle to upper (table is symmetric)
 matrix = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(n)]
 for i in range(n):
 for j in range(n):
 if rows[i][j]:
 matrix[i][j] = rows[i][j]
 elif j < len(rows) and i < len(rows[j]) and rows[j][i]:
 matrix[i][j] = rows[j][i]
 return matrix, address_to_index

Edge list (less common)

EDGE LIST
Just a list of (u, v, weight) triples — no organization by vertex.

Pros: simple; great for Kruskal's MST (sort all edges).
Cons: O(E) to find any specific edge or neighbors.

Use case: when you'll iterate ALL edges (sorting, Kruskal, edge-based algorithms).

Special cases — implicit graphs

IMPLICIT GRAPHS
Sometimes the graph isn't stored explicitly — it's defined by a function.

Grid graphs (mazes): vertex = cell; neighbors = computed by adjacency rules.
Game state graphs: vertex = state; neighbors = legal moves.
Web crawlers: vertex = URL; neighbors = links found by fetching.

No explicit storage — the graph is generated on demand.

Directed vs undirected — implementation differences

DIRECTED EDGE
Add (u → v) only:
Matrix: M[u][v] = weight
List: adj[u].append((v, weight))
UNDIRECTED EDGE
Add (u → v) AND (v → u):
Matrix: M[u][v] = M[v][u] = weight
List: adj[u].append((v, weight)); adj[v].append((u, weight))

Parcel Service distances are SYMMETRIC (undirected).

"I represent the Parcel Service distance table as an ADJACENCY MATRIX — a 27 × 27 grid of float distances. Since the distance table is COMPLETE (a value exists for every address pair), the graph is dense and an adjacency matrix wastes no space. Edge weight lookup is O(1), critical for the inner loop of the nearest-neighbor routing algorithm.

An adjacency list would have used more memory due to per-bucket overhead and slower O(deg(u)) lookups. For a sparser graph (e.g., a real-world road network with only adjacent intersections connected), I would have chosen an adjacency list."

BFS and DFS are the two foundational graph traversal algorithms. Every other graph algorithm — Dijkstra, topological sort, MST, connected components — builds on one or the other. The OA tests choosing between them, tracing executions, and recognizing what each is good for.

BFS — Breadth-First Search

BFS
Explore vertices in LAYERS by distance from the start.
Visit all neighbors at distance 1, then all at distance 2, then 3, ...

Uses a QUEUE (FIFO) — first vertex enqueued is first to be processed.

Time: O(V + E). Space: O(V) for the queue and visited set. 
from collections import deque

def bfs(graph, start):
 """Standard BFS. Returns dict of {vertex: distance from start}."""
 distances = {start: 0}
 queue = deque([start])
 while queue:
 current = queue.popleft()
 for neighbor in graph.neighbors(current):
 if neighbor not in distances:
 distances[neighbor] = distances[current] + 1
 queue.append(neighbor)
 return distances
BFS PROPERTIES
✓ Finds the SHORTEST path (in unweighted graphs).
✓ Visits vertices in order of increasing distance from start.
✓ Naturally builds a "level structure" of the graph.
✗ Uses more memory than DFS for shallow trees (queue grows wide).

BFS use cases

WHEN BFS SHINES
Shortest path in unweighted graph: BFS finds it in O(V + E).
Level-order tree traversal: BFS gives top-to-bottom, left-to-right.
Connected components: BFS from each unvisited vertex.
Bipartiteness check: 2-coloring via BFS levels.
Web crawling (limited depth): BFS to a fixed level.
Social network "degrees of separation": BFS from a person.
GPS navigation (with weights → use Dijkstra instead).

DFS — Depth-First Search

DFS
Go DEEP first — follow one path as far as possible, then backtrack.

Uses a STACK (LIFO) — explicitly via stack data structure or implicitly via recursion.

Time: O(V + E). Space: O(V) for the recursion stack and visited set. 
def dfs_recursive(graph, start, visited=None):
 """Standard DFS via recursion."""
 if visited is None:
 visited = set()
 visited.add(start)
 for neighbor in graph.neighbors(start):
 if neighbor not in visited:
 dfs_recursive(graph, neighbor, visited)
 return visited

def dfs_iterative(graph, start):
 """DFS via explicit stack."""
 visited = set()
 stack = [start]
 while stack:
 current = stack.pop()
 if current in visited:
 continue
 visited.add(current)
 for neighbor in graph.neighbors(current):
 if neighbor not in visited:
 stack.append(neighbor)
 return visited
DFS PROPERTIES
✓ Less memory than BFS for deep narrow graphs.
✓ Naturally detects cycles (revisiting a vertex on the current path).
✓ Generates a "DFS tree" — useful for many algorithms.
✗ Does NOT find shortest paths.
✗ Recursive version can stack-overflow on deep graphs.

DFS use cases

WHEN DFS SHINES
Cycle detection: a back-edge in DFS tree = cycle.
Topological sort: DFS post-order reversed gives topo order.
Strongly connected components (Tarjan's, Kosaraju's): both use DFS.
Solving puzzles via backtracking: maze, Sudoku, N-Queens.
Finding articulation points and bridges: DFS-based.
Spanning tree: DFS gives one (any DFS).
Path existence: DFS reaches everything reachable from start.
