Topological sort via DFS

TOPOLOGICAL SORT
Linear ordering of vertices in a DAG such that every edge u → v has u BEFORE v.

Used for: dependency resolution (build systems, course prerequisites, Excel formulas).

Algorithm: DFS, then reverse the post-order. 
def topological_sort(graph, vertices):
 visited = set()
 stack = []

 def dfs(v):
 visited.add(v)
 for neighbor in graph.neighbors(v):
 if neighbor not in visited:
 dfs(neighbor)
 stack.append(v) # post-order: v added AFTER all descendants

 for v in vertices:
 if v not in visited:
 dfs(v)

 return stack[::-1] # reverse for topo order

Cycle detection via DFS

def has_cycle(graph, vertices):
 """Detect cycle in directed graph via DFS coloring."""
 WHITE, GRAY, BLACK = 0, 1, 2
 color = {v: WHITE for v in vertices}

 def dfs(v):
 color[v] = GRAY # currently visiting
 for neighbor in graph.neighbors(v):
 if color[neighbor] == GRAY:
 return True # back-edge to GRAY ancestor → cycle!
 if color[neighbor] == WHITE and dfs(neighbor):
 return True
 color[v] = BLACK # fully done
 return False

 for v in vertices:
 if color[v] == WHITE:
 if dfs(v):
 return True
 return False

 # BFS or DFS from v

Neither BFS nor DFS is the routing algorithm for Parcel Service — that's nearest-neighbor (covered earlier). However:

DFS would explore one route deeply, also not yielding minimum distance. For weighted shortest paths, Dijkstra's algorithm is the right choice; for the TSP-style routing required by Parcel Service, the nearest-neighbor heuristic outperforms naive BFS/DFS."

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Dijkstra is THE canonical shortest-path algorithm — used in Google Maps, network routing protocols (OSPF), GPS navigation, and game AI. The OA tests both the trace (running Dijkstra by hand on a small graph) and the underlying intuition (greedy choice, priority queue, why non-negative weights matter). For the Parcel Service PA, Dijkstra could compute optimal point-to-point routes if the routing problem were SSSP instead of TSP.

The shortest-path problem

SHORTEST PATH VARIANTS
Single-source shortest path (SSSP): from one source to ALL other vertices.
Single-pair shortest path: from one source to one destination.
All-pairs shortest path (APSP): from every vertex to every other.

Dijkstra solves SSSP in O((V + E) log V) on graphs with non-negative weights.

Dijkstra's algorithm — core idea

CORE INSIGHT
Greedily extend the "settled" set of vertices (whose shortest distance is known).
At each step, pick the UNSETTLED vertex with the smallest tentative distance and mark it settled.
Update tentative distances of its neighbors.
Repeat until all vertices are settled.

The greedy choice is provably optimal because non-negative weights mean we can never "improve" a settled vertex via a longer path.

Dijkstra pseudocode

PSEUDOCODE
function Dijkstra(graph, source):
  dist[source] = 0; dist[v] = INF for all other v
  visited = empty set
  min_heap = priority queue with (0, source)
  while min_heap not empty:
    (d, u) = min_heap.pop() # smallest tentative distance
    if u in visited: continue
    visited.add(u)
    for each neighbor v of u with edge weight w:
      if d + w < dist[v]: # found shorter path
       dist[v] = d + w
       min_heap.push((dist[v], v))
  return dist

Python implementation with heap

import heapq

def dijkstra(graph, source):
 """SSSP via Dijkstra. Returns dict of {vertex: shortest distance from source}."""
 dist = {v: float('inf') for v in graph.vertices()}
 dist[source] = 0
 visited = set()
 heap = [(0, source)] # (tentative distance, vertex)

 while heap:
 d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
 if u in visited:
 continue
 visited.add(u)
 for v, weight in graph.neighbors_with_weights(u):
 new_dist = d + weight
 if new_dist < dist[v]:
 dist[v] = new_dist
 heapq.heappush(heap, (new_dist, v))

 return dist

def dijkstra_with_path(graph, source, target):
 """Return shortest path from source to target as a list of vertices."""
 dist = {v: float('inf') for v in graph.vertices()}
 dist[source] = 0
 prev = {v: None for v in graph.vertices()}
 visited = set()
 heap = [(0, source)]

 while heap:
 d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
 if u in visited:
 continue
 visited.add(u)
 if u == target:
 break
 for v, weight in graph.neighbors_with_weights(u):
 new_dist = d + weight
 if new_dist < dist[v]:
 dist[v] = new_dist
 prev[v] = u
 heapq.heappush(heap, (new_dist, v))

 # Reconstruct path
 path = []
 current = target
 while current is not None:
 path.append(current)
 current = prev[current]
 return list(reversed(path)), dist[target]

Why non-negative weights?

DIJKSTRA REQUIRES NON-NEGATIVE WEIGHTS
Once a vertex is settled, Dijkstra never reconsiders it.
This is safe BECAUSE non-negative edges mean any future path via the settled vertex would be at least as long — never shorter.

With negative weights, this assumption breaks. A "longer" path through a negative edge could actually be shorter. Use Bellman-Ford (next section) instead.

Complexity

DIJKSTRA COMPLEXITY
With binary heap: O((V + E) log V).
With Fibonacci heap: O(E + V log V) — theoretically faster but rarely worth it in practice.
Without heap (linear scan): O(V²) — simpler but slow for sparse graphs.

For dense graphs, O(V²) is competitive because E ≈ V².

Dijkstra optimizations

PRACTICAL OPTIMIZATIONS
Early termination: stop when you settle the target vertex.
Bidirectional Dijkstra: search from source AND target simultaneously.
A* algorithm: Dijkstra + heuristic estimate to target → much faster on geographic graphs.
Contraction hierarchies: precompute shortcuts → microsecond queries on continent-scale road networks.

A* — Dijkstra plus a heuristic

A* ALGORITHM
Same as Dijkstra but uses priority = (current distance + heuristic estimate to target).
Heuristic must be ADMISSIBLE (never overestimates true distance).

For geographic data, straight-line distance is a great heuristic.
A* dramatically reduces nodes explored vs Dijkstra when heading toward a single target.

Dijkstra applications

REAL-WORLD USES
GPS routing: shortest road path (with A* heuristic).
OSPF / IS-IS: internet routing protocols.
Network bandwidth optimization: shortest hops or cheapest cost.
Game AI pathfinding: A* on grid graphs (most games).
Telephone routing: cheapest call path.
Robot motion planning: shortest collision-free path.

Could Dijkstra be used for Parcel Service?

Parcel Service RELEVANCE
Parcel Service asks for a TSP-style ROUTE (visit all addresses), not a single shortest path.
Dijkstra solves "from hub to address X, what's the shortest path?" — not "what's the shortest tour visiting all addresses?"

However, Dijkstra IS used to compute pairwise distances IF the input were a road network rather than a complete distance matrix. For Parcel Service, the distance matrix is GIVEN, so Dijkstra isn't needed.

Mention in Section F: "Dijkstra solves SSSP, not TSP. For Parcel Service routing, NN is appropriate; for individual delivery navigation given a road graph, Dijkstra (or A*) would compute optimal road paths."
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Using Dijkstra with negative edge weights — produces wrong answers. Use Bellman-Ford.

Forgetting the visited check — popping the same vertex multiple times wastes work.

Using a regular queue or stack — Dijkstra needs a priority queue (min-heap).

Missing the "if d + w < dist[v]" relaxation — without this you visit every edge multiple times.

Decreasing-key in the heap is hard in Python — easier to push duplicates and check visited.

Treating Dijkstra as solving TSP — it doesn't.

★ ON THE OA

"Dijkstra time complexity?" → O((V + E) log V) with heap.

"What does Dijkstra need that Bellman-Ford doesn't?" → non-negative weights.

"Trace Dijkstra step by step" → settle smallest-tentative-distance vertex, relax edges.

"What data structure does Dijkstra use?" → min-heap (priority queue).

"Difference between Dijkstra and BFS?" → Dijkstra handles weights; BFS is unweighted.

"A* vs Dijkstra?" → A* adds a heuristic for faster targeted search.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Dijkstra solves single-source shortest path on non-negative weights
  • Greedy: settle nearest unvisited vertex, relax its edges
  • Uses a min-heap (priority queue)
  • Time: O((V + E) log V) with binary heap
  • FAILS on negative weights — use Bellman-Ford instead
  • Real uses: GPS, OSPF routing, game AI pathfinding
  • A* extends Dijkstra with a heuristic for faster goal-directed search
  • For Parcel Service: not the routing algorithm (TSP, not SSSP), but COULD compute pairwise distances
🧠 MEMORY AID

Dijkstra = greedy + min-heap, and ONLY for non-negative weights. Repeatedly pull the closest unvisited vertex and relax its edges. If the graph can have negative weights, use Bellman-Ford (which also detects negative cycles). For fewest-edges in an unweighted graph, plain BFS already gives the shortest path.

★ ON THE OA / PA — WATCH FOR

Dijkstra finds shortest paths from a source in a non-negative weighted graph, greedily settling the closest unsettled vertex (min-priority queue). Fails with NEGATIVE edges. OA: Dijkstra needs non-negative weights; complexity O((V+E) log V).

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
dist[src]=0, others=inf; pop min, relax neighbors:
if dist[u]+w < dist[v]: dist[v]=dist[u]+w

Result: greedy relaxation → shortest paths

Dijkstra assumes reaching a vertex can't get cheaper later — false with negative edges, which is why Bellman-Ford exists. Know the restriction.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

When Dijkstra fails — typically because a graph has negative-weight edges — Bellman-Ford steps in. It's slower (O(V·E) vs O((V+E) log V)) but handles negative weights and detects negative cycles. Topological sort is the other essential graph-traversal-derived algorithm: it linearizes a DAG into an order that respects all dependencies. Both appear on the OA as conceptual questions and small traces.

Bellman-Ford — handles negative weights

BELLMAN-FORD ALGORITHM
Solves single-source shortest path on graphs with NEGATIVE edge weights (no negative cycles).
Also DETECTS negative cycles (returns "no shortest path exists" if found).

Idea: relax EVERY edge V−1 times. After V−1 iterations, all shortest paths are found.
One more iteration: if any distance still decreases, there's a negative cycle.

Bellman-Ford pseudocode

def bellman_ford(graph, source):
 """SSSP via Bellman-Ford. Returns dist dict, or None if negative cycle."""
 dist = {v: float('inf') for v in graph.vertices()}
 dist[source] = 0

 # Relax every edge V-1 times
 for _ in range(len(graph.vertices()) - 1):
 for (u, v, weight) in graph.edges():
 if dist[u] + weight < dist[v]:
 dist[v] = dist[u] + weight

 # Check for negative cycle
 for (u, v, weight) in graph.edges():
 if dist[u] + weight < dist[v]:
 return None # negative cycle detected

 return dist
COMPLEXITY
Time: O(V · E) — V−1 iterations × E edges per iteration.
Space: O(V) for the distance array.

Slower than Dijkstra's O((V + E) log V), but handles negative weights.

Why V−1 iterations?

PROOF SKETCH
A shortest path has at most V−1 edges (no cycles in shortest paths).
Each iteration extends the "reach" by one edge.
After V−1 iterations, all reachable vertices have correct shortest distances.
A V-th iteration shouldn't change anything UNLESS a negative cycle allows infinite improvement.

StrategyGreedy + heapDP / repeated relaxation
Distributed?HardEasy (RIP routing protocol)
Best forStandard SSSP, GPSNegative weights, RIP

Negative cycles — what they mean

NEGATIVE CYCLE
A cycle whose edge weights sum to a NEGATIVE number.
Each traversal makes the path shorter — no minimum exists.

Real-world examples:
Currency arbitrage: a sequence of currency exchanges that returns more than you started with.
Energy systems: a loop that produces net energy (would violate physics, but appears in modeling errors).
Bellman-Ford detects these — a security feature for arbitrage analysis.

Topological sort

TOPOLOGICAL SORT
Linear ordering of DAG vertices such that every edge u → v has u BEFORE v in the ordering.

Used wherever there are dependencies:
  Course prerequisites (take Math 101 before Math 201)
  Build systems (compile A.c before linking with B.o)
  Spreadsheet formula evaluation (recompute base cells first)
  Task scheduling with precedence
  Package install order (apt-get, npm)

Two algorithms for topological sort

Algorithm 1: DFS-based

def topo_sort_dfs(graph):
 visited = set()
 stack = []

 def dfs(v):
 visited.add(v)
 for neighbor in graph.neighbors(v):
 if neighbor not in visited:
 dfs(neighbor)
 stack.append(v) # post-order

 for v in graph.vertices():
 if v not in visited:
 dfs(v)

 return stack[::-1] # reverse for topo order

Algorithm 2: Kahn's algorithm (BFS-based)

from collections import deque

def topo_sort_kahn(graph):
 """Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly remove nodes with no incoming edges."""
 # Compute in-degree of every vertex
 in_degree = {v: 0 for v in graph.vertices()}
 for u in graph.vertices():
 for v in graph.neighbors(u):
 in_degree[v] += 1

 # Start with vertices having no incoming edges
 queue = deque([v for v in graph.vertices() if in_degree[v] == 0])
 result = []

 while queue:
 u = queue.popleft()
 result.append(u)
 for v in graph.neighbors(u):
 in_degree[v] -= 1
 if in_degree[v] == 0:
 queue.append(v)

 if len(result) != len(graph.vertices()):
 return None # cycle detected (not a DAG)

 return result
KAHN'S ALGORITHM INTUITION
Vertices with NO incoming edges have no prerequisites — emit them first.
Once emitted, "remove" them by decrementing incoming counts of their neighbors.
Newly-zero-in-degree vertices become emittable.
If we run out before emitting all vertices: the graph has a cycle.

Iteration orderReverse post-orderLayer by layer
Easier to parallelizeNoYes

Topological sort and cycles

CYCLE DETECTION
Topological sort EXISTS ⟺ the graph is a DAG (no cycles).

If topo sort fails to emit all vertices: there's a cycle.
If you need just cycle detection in a DAG context: try topo sort and check the result length.

Real-world topological sort applications

USE CASES
Build systems: Make, Bazel, Gradle compute build order via topo sort.
Package managers: apt-get, npm, pip resolve install order.
Spreadsheet recalc: Excel, Google Sheets recompute cells in topo order.

Bellman-Ford applications

USE CASES
Routing Information Protocol (RIP): classic distance-vector network protocol.
Currency arbitrage detection: negative cycle = arbitrage opportunity.
Network analysis with penalties/refunds: edges can have negative cost.
Shortest path with constraints: when costs aren't just positive distances.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Using Dijkstra on a graph with negative edges — produces wrong answers silently.

Stopping Bellman-Ford early — must do exactly V−1 iterations.

Forgetting the negative-cycle check (the V-th iteration).

Trying to topo-sort a graph with cycles — no valid ordering exists.

Confusing topo-sort with sorted order (numerical / alphabetical) — topo respects DEPENDENCIES.

In Kahn's: forgetting to handle multiple "ready" vertices — pick one or process them in parallel.

★ ON THE OA

"Bellman-Ford complexity?" → O(V · E).

"How does Bellman-Ford detect a negative cycle?" → run a V-th iteration; if anything still decreases, cycle exists.

"Topological sort precondition?" → graph must be a DAG (no cycles).

"Topo sort applications?" → build systems, package managers, course prerequisites.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Bellman-Ford: SSSP with negative weights, O(V · E)
  • Relax every edge V−1 times; one more iteration detects negative cycles
  • Topological sort: linear order respecting all directed edges
  • Only works on DAGs; cycle detection is a free byproduct
  • Two algorithms: DFS post-order reversed, OR Kahn's via in-degree counting
  • Both topo algorithms: O(V + E)
  • Applications: build systems, package managers, spreadsheet recalc, course planning
  • Bellman-Ford is the basis of RIP routing protocol
★ ON THE OA / PA — WATCH FOR

Bellman-Ford handles NEGATIVE edges and detects negative cycles, O(V·E). Topological sort orders a DAG so every edge points forward (via DFS finish-times or Kahn's in-degree queue). OA: which algorithm for negative weights (Bellman-Ford) and topo-sort needs a DAG.

Bellman-Ford: relax ALL edges V-1 times;
a V-th relaxation that still improves = negative cycle

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Minimum spanning trees (MSTs) solve a huge family of network-design problems: laying minimum-cost cable to connect all houses, designing electrical grids, single-linkage clustering. Two famous greedy algorithms find MSTs: Kruskal's (sorted edges + union-find) and Prim's (grow from a vertex via heap). The OA tests both algorithm choice and traceability. Both are PROVABLY OPTIMAL — the rare case where greedy gives the exact answer.

Spanning trees

SPANNING TREE
A subgraph of a connected graph G that:
  1. Includes EVERY vertex of G,
  2. Is a tree (connected, acyclic), and
  3. Has exactly V − 1 edges.

Every connected graph has at least one spanning tree (often many).

Minimum spanning tree (MST)

MST
Given a connected, weighted, undirected graph, the minimum spanning tree is a spanning tree whose total edge weight is minimum.

Two famous greedy algorithms find it: Kruskal's and Prim's.
Both are PROVABLY OPTIMAL.

Kruskal's algorithm — edge-based greedy

def kruskal(graph):
 """Build MST via Kruskal's. Returns list of MST edges."""
 edges = sorted(graph.edges(), key=lambda e: e[2]) # sort by weight
 uf = UnionFind(graph.vertices())
 mst = []
 for u, v, weight in edges:
 if uf.find(u) != uf.find(v): # adding doesn't create cycle
 uf.union(u, v)
 mst.append((u, v, weight))
 if len(mst) == len(graph.vertices()) - 1:
 break # done
 return mst
KRUSKAL — STEP BY STEP
1. Sort all edges by weight ascending.
2. Initialize MST as empty.
3. For each edge in sorted order:
  If adding it wouldn't create a cycle (Union-Find check), add it.
4. Stop when MST has V − 1 edges.

Time: O(E log E) — sorting dominates.

Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union, DSU)

UNION-FIND
Data structure that tracks which vertices are in the same component.
Two operations:
  find(u) — return the representative of u's component.
  union(u, v) — merge u and v's components.

With "path compression" + "union by rank," both operations are O(α(n)) ≈ O(1) — practically constant. 
class UnionFind:
 def __init__(self, vertices):
 self.parent = {v: v for v in vertices}
 self.rank = {v: 0 for v in vertices}

 def find(self, u):
 # Path compression: link directly to root
 if self.parent[u] != u:
 self.parent[u] = self.find(self.parent[u])
 return self.parent[u]

 def union(self, u, v):
 root_u = self.find(u)
 root_v = self.find(v)
 if root_u == root_v:
 return False
 # Union by rank: smaller tree under larger
 if self.rank[root_u] < self.rank[root_v]:
 self.parent[root_u] = root_v
 elif self.rank[root_u] > self.rank[root_v]:
 self.parent[root_v] = root_u
 else:
 self.parent[root_v] = root_u
 self.rank[root_u] += 1
 return True

Prim's algorithm — vertex-based greedy

import heapq

def prim(graph, start):
 """Build MST via Prim's. Returns list of MST edges."""
 in_tree = {start}
 mst = []
 # Heap of edges crossing the tree
 heap = [(weight, start, v) for v, weight in graph.neighbors_with_weights(start)]
 heapq.heapify(heap)

 while heap and len(in_tree) < len(graph.vertices()):
 weight, u, v = heapq.heappop(heap)
 if v in in_tree:
 continue
 in_tree.add(v)
 mst.append((u, v, weight))
 # Add v's edges to candidates
 for next_v, next_weight in graph.neighbors_with_weights(v):
 if next_v not in in_tree:
 heapq.heappush(heap, (next_weight, v, next_v))

 return mst
PRIM — STEP BY STEP
1. Start at any vertex; mark it "in tree."
2. Repeat V − 1 times:
  Among edges with one endpoint in tree, one outside, pick the cheapest.
  Add it to MST. Add the new vertex to tree.
3. Done when all vertices are in the tree.

Time: O(E log V) with binary heap; O(E + V log V) with Fibonacci heap.

Why both algorithms work — cut and cycle properties

CUT PROPERTY
For any cut (S, V−S) of the graph, the minimum-weight edge crossing the cut is in some MST.
→ Justifies Prim's: add cheapest edge crossing the current "tree vs not-tree" cut.
CYCLE PROPERTY
For any cycle in the graph, the maximum-weight edge in the cycle is NOT in any MST.
→ Justifies Kruskal: skipping cycle-creating edges is safe.

MST uniqueness

UNIQUENESS
If all edge weights are distinct, the MST is UNIQUE.
If some weights tie, multiple MSTs may exist (all with same total weight).

Both Kruskal and Prim find SOME MST — possibly different ones if ties exist — but always optimal total weight.

MST gives the cheapest "tree" connecting all addresses — but a tree is NOT a route. A route must visit each address ONCE and return (a TOUR / cycle).

For Parcel Service Section F: "MST + DFS tour gives a 2-approximation for TSP. While interesting, nearest-neighbor is simpler to implement and produces routes well within the 140-mile constraint, so I chose NN."

Why hash tables exist

Anatomy of a hash table

The full skeleton (for OA conceptual questions)

class HashTable:
 def __init__(self, capacity=53):
 self.capacity = capacity
 self.size = 0
 self.buckets = [None] * capacity # or [[]] * capacity for chaining

 def _hash(self, key):
 return hash(key) % self.capacity # or your custom hash

 def insert(self, key, value):
 index = self._hash(key)
 # Collision handling logic (chaining or probing) goes here
 ...
 self.size += 1
 if self.size / self.capacity > 0.75:
 self._resize(self.capacity * 2)

 def lookup(self, key):
 index = self._hash(key)
 # Collision handling lookup
 ...

 def _resize(self, new_capacity):
 old_buckets = self.buckets
 self.capacity = new_capacity
 self.size = 0
 self.buckets = [None] * new_capacity
 for entry in old_buckets:
 if entry is not None:
 # Re-insert each entry (rehashes with new capacity)
 ...

Load factor and resizing

LOAD FACTOR
α = size / capacity

Low α (e.g., 0.3): lots of empty buckets, fast lookups, wasted space.
High α (e.g., 0.9): many collisions, slow lookups.
Sweet spot: 0.5 - 0.75. Most implementations resize at 0.75.

When α exceeds threshold:
  1. Allocate a new array, typically 2× current capacity.
  2. Iterate over OLD buckets, rehashing each key into the NEW array.
  3. Replace old array with new.

Cost of resize: O(n). But amortized over many inserts, average insert is still O(1).

Why resizing is "self-adjusting"

The rubric in C950 calls for a "self-adjusting data structure." The hash table qualifies because:

  1. It MEASURES its own state (load factor).
  2. It REACTS to that state (resize when threshold crossed).
  3. It MAINTAINS its O(1) average performance under varying input sizes.

✗ Using a non-deterministic hash (e.g., random) — breaks the table.
✗ Resizing only when "full" (load factor 1.0) — lookups become very slow.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Two keys can hash to the same bucket — that's a collision. How you handle it defines the personality of your hash table. The two main approaches are CHAINING (each bucket holds a list) and OPEN ADDRESSING (find another bucket). For the C950 PA, chaining is overwhelmingly the right choice — simpler, more forgiving, and easier to defend in your write-up.

The collision problem

Hash functions map an arbitrary key space to a fixed-size index range. The pigeonhole principle GUARANTEES collisions when the key space exceeds the bucket count. Even with low load factors, collisions happen — the birthday paradox tells us that with just 23 keys hashing into 365 buckets, there's already a 50% chance of a collision.

Chaining (separate chaining)

CHAINING
Each bucket is a LIST (or linked list) of [key, value] pairs.
Multiple entries with the same hash live together in the same bucket's list.
Lookup: hash key, scan bucket's list for matching key.

Pros: simple, handles arbitrary load factors gracefully, easy to delete.
Cons: extra memory for list overhead per bucket.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Chaining 4 keys into 4 buckets

Keys 5, 12, 9, 21. Capacity 4. hash = key % 4.

1
Insert 5 → hash 1 → bucket 1: [[5, val5]]
📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
2
Insert 12 → hash 0 → bucket 0: [[12, val12]]
3
Insert 9 → hash 1 → bucket 1 (collision!): 5val59val9
4
Insert 21 → hash 1 → bucket 1 (another collision): 5val59val921val21
✓
Final state: bucket 0 = [[12]], bucket 1 = 5921, buckets 2, 3 empty.

Chaining implementation (Python)

class ChainingHashTable:
 def __init__(self, capacity=53):
 self.capacity = capacity
 self.size = 0
 self.buckets = [[] for _ in range(capacity)] # one empty list per bucket

 def _hash(self, key):
 return int(key) % self.capacity

 def insert(self, key, value):
 bucket = self.buckets[self._hash(key)]
 for kv in bucket:
 if kv[0] == key:
 kv[1] = value # update existing
 return
 bucket.append([key, value])
 self.size += 1

 def lookup(self, key):
 bucket = self.buckets[self._hash(key)]
 for kv in bucket:
 if kv[0] == key:
 return kv[1]
 return None

 def remove(self, key):
 bucket = self.buckets[self._hash(key)]
 for i, kv in enumerate(bucket):
 if kv[0] == key:
 bucket.pop(i)
 self.size -= 1
 return True
 return False

Open addressing

OPEN ADDRESSING
Each bucket holds at most ONE entry.
On collision, PROBE other buckets (using a probe sequence) until an empty slot is found.
Lookup: hash key, then probe until matching key found OR empty slot found.

Pros: better cache performance, no extra list overhead.
Cons: deletion is awkward (need tombstones), max load factor < 1.0, harder to implement correctly.

Three open-addressing probe strategies

LINEAR PROBING
If bucket i is occupied, try i + 1, i + 2, i + 3, ... (mod capacity).

Pros: simple, cache-friendly.
Cons: PRIMARY CLUSTERING — clusters of consecutive occupied buckets grow.
QUADRATIC PROBING
If bucket i is occupied, try i + 1², i + 2², i + 3², ... = i+1, i+4, i+9, i+16 (mod capacity).

Pros: avoids primary clustering.
Cons: SECONDARY CLUSTERING (keys hashing to same bucket follow same probe sequence). Doesn't always cover all buckets.
DOUBLE HASHING
If bucket i is occupied, try i + 1·h₂(key), i + 2·h₂(key), ..., where h₂ is a second hash function.

Pros: best collision distribution.
Cons: most complex to implement.

Comparison table

AspectChainingOpen Addressing
Load factor > 1?Yes, fineNo, must resize
Memory overheadList per bucketJust bucket array
Cache performanceWorse (pointers)Better (contiguous)
DeletionEasy (remove from list)Hard (need tombstones)
Implementation complexitySimpleMore complex
Worst-case lookupO(n) (one big chain)O(n) (long probe)
Used in productionJava HashMapPython dict, .NET

Why chaining wins for the C950 PA

RECOMMENDED CHOICE: CHAINING
✓ Simpler to implement → fewer bugs → faster to PA submission.
✓ Easier to explain in the write-up (Section A).
✓ Easy to delete and update entries.
✓ Handles any load factor without immediate breakage.
✓ For 40 packages, performance differences are irrelevant.
✓ Most Reddit guides and CI examples use chaining.

The tombstone problem (open addressing only)

If you DELETE an entry in open addressing by just zeroing the bucket, future lookups for collided keys may stop early at that empty slot and miss the keys further along the probe sequence.

TOMBSTONE FIX
Mark deleted entries with a special "tombstone" value (not empty, not occupied).
Lookups: continue probing past tombstones.
Inserts: can reuse tombstone slots.

Adds complexity. Periodic rehash to remove tombstones is needed.

What to write in your PA Section A justification

SECTION A LANGUAGE
"I selected SEPARATE CHAINING over open addressing because: (1) chaining is simpler to implement and reason about, reducing the risk of bugs that would compromise package lookups; (2) the Parcel Service use case requires occasional UPDATES to package status, which chaining supports trivially while open addressing requires careful tombstone handling; (3) chaining tolerates higher load factors without performance cliffs, providing safer behavior if the package count grows; (4) for the 40-package Parcel Service data set, the performance difference between chaining and open addressing is negligible."

Performance under collisions

EXPECTED CHAIN LENGTH
Under uniform hashing, average chain length = α (load factor).
α = 0.5 → average chain ≈ 0.5 entries — most buckets are empty or have 1 entry.
α = 0.75 → average chain ≈ 0.75 entries.
α = 1.0 → average chain ≈ 1 entry — everything still fast.

In the WORST case (all keys collide), chain length = n. Hence O(n) worst-case.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Initializing buckets with [[]] * capacity in Python — all share the same list! Use [[] for _ in range(capacity)].

Open addressing without tombstones — deletion silently breaks future lookups.

Linear probing with poor hash → primary clustering → many slow lookups.

Forgetting to handle "key already exists" on insert — silent duplicate vs intended update.

Using open addressing for the PA when chaining is simpler and equally effective.

Chaining = list per bucket. Open addressing = single entry per bucket.

Linear probing has primary clustering. Quadratic has secondary. Double hashing distributes best.

Java HashMap uses chaining (with tree fallback for huge buckets in Java 8+).

Python dict uses open addressing with perturbation.

For the PA: chaining is the safer choice.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Collisions are inevitable — handle gracefully
  • Chaining: list per bucket, simple, supports α > 1, easy delete
  • Open addressing: probe sequence, better cache, complex delete
  • Linear probing → primary clustering
  • Quadratic probing → secondary clustering
  • Double hashing → best distribution, most complex
  • For C950 PA: USE CHAINING — simpler and sufficient
  • Java HashMap = chaining; Python dict = open addressing
  • Average chain length = load factor α (uniform hashing)

For the PA, chaining is simplest and never overflows (each bucket is a list); open addressing needs resize logic and free slots. With ~40 packages a small table with chaining keeps lookups near O(1). OA: chaining vs open addressing trade-offs.

The insert operation

def insert(self, key, value):
 """
 Insert (key, value). If key exists, update its value.
 Average O(1), worst O(n).
 """
 bucket_index = self._hash(key)
 bucket = self.buckets[bucket_index]

 # Check for existing key — update if found
 for entry in bucket:
 if entry[0] == key:
 entry[1] = value # update existing value
 return

 # New key — append
 bucket.append([key, value])
 self.size += 1

 # Optional: trigger resize if load factor too high
 if self.size / self.capacity > 0.75:
 self._resize(self.capacity * 2)
INSERT BEHAVIOR REQUIREMENTS
✓ If key doesn't exist → ADD entry, increment size.
✓ If key already exists → UPDATE value, leave size unchanged.
✓ Trigger resize if load factor exceeds threshold (e.g., 0.75).
✓ Returns nothing (void) — caller doesn't need confirmation.

The lookup operation (Section B of rubric!)

def lookup(self, key):
 """
 Look up package by key. Return Package object or None if not found.
 Returns the FULL package — caller can access all fields.
 Average O(1), worst O(n).
 """
 bucket_index = self._hash(key)
 bucket = self.buckets[bucket_index]

 for entry in bucket:
 if entry[0] == key:
 return entry[1] # the Package object

 return None # not found
LOOKUP REQUIREMENTS (FROM RUBRIC SECTION B)
Look-up function MUST return a Package containing ALL fields:
  ✓ Delivery address
  ✓ Delivery deadline
  ✓ Delivery city
  ✓ Delivery zip code
  ✓ Package weight
  ✓ Delivery status (with timestamp updates)

Returning just the address (or any subset) FAILS Section B.

The update operation

The hash table doesn't need a separate `update` — your `insert` already updates if the key exists. But you need to UPDATE PACKAGE FIELDS as the day progresses (status changes, delivery times). Here's how:

def update_package_status(hash_table, package_id, new_status, current_time):
 """Update a package's status mid-simulation."""
 pkg = hash_table.lookup(package_id)
 if pkg is None:
 raise ValueError(f"Package {package_id} not found")

 pkg.status = new_status
 if new_status == "EN_ROUTE":
 pkg.departed_hub_time = current_time
 elif new_status == "DELIVERED":
 pkg.delivered_time = current_time
 # The Package object is referenced by the table, so the update is
 # automatically reflected in future lookups. No re-insert needed.

Critical Python gotcha — mutable references

REFERENCE SEMANTICS
Python stores OBJECT REFERENCES, not copies, in your hash table.

When you modify pkg.status, the change is visible from any future lookup() because lookup returns the SAME object reference.

This is GOOD — no need to re-insert after updating fields.

Handling the wrong-address package

One package in the Parcel Service data has an INCORRECT address that gets corrected at 10:20 AM. Here's how to handle it:

def update_wrong_address(hash_table, current_time):
 """Apply the address correction at 10:20 AM."""

 pkg = hash_table.lookup(9) # or whichever ID has the issue
 if pkg.notes.startswith("Wrong address"):
 pkg.address = "410 S State St"
 pkg.city = "Salt Lake City"
 pkg.state = "UT"
 pkg.zip = "84111"
 pkg.notes = pkg.notes + " — corrected at 10:20 AM"

def get_status_at_time(package, query_time):
 """
 Return human-readable status of a package at the given time.

 return f"En route on truck {package.truck_id}"

def all_packages(self):

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Huffman coding is the classic data-compression algorithm and a beautiful application of greedy strategy on a binary tree. Used inside ZIP, JPEG, MP3, and many other formats. The OA tests building Huffman trees, generating codes, and computing compression ratios. The algorithm itself is a perfect illustration of greedy choice + optimal substructure: the rare combination that makes greedy provably optimal.

The compression problem

FIXED-LENGTH ENCODING
ASCII assigns 8 bits per character — every character takes the SAME space.

Wasteful: rare characters use the same space as common ones. "z" and "e" both take 8 bits, even though "e" appears 10× more often.
VARIABLE-LENGTH ENCODING
Assign FEWER bits to common characters, MORE to rare ones.
Total file size shrinks if the encoding is well-chosen.

Catch: must be UNIQUELY DECODABLE — given a stream of bits, you must be able to recover the original characters unambiguously.

Prefix codes

PREFIX CODE
An encoding where no codeword is a PREFIX of any other.

Example (valid prefix code):
  a = 0
  b = 10
  c = 110
  d = 111

No codeword starts with another codeword → unambiguous decoding.
Counter-example: a = 0, b = 01 — bad! "01" could be "ab" or "b."

Huffman tree

HUFFMAN TREE
A BINARY TREE where:
  Each LEAF represents a character + frequency.
  Each INTERNAL node has frequency = sum of children's frequencies.
  Codeword for a leaf = path from root: 0 = left, 1 = right.

By construction, no codeword is a prefix of another.

Building a Huffman tree

HUFFMAN ALGORITHM
1. Compute frequency of each character.
2. Create a leaf node for each, insert into a MIN-HEAP keyed by frequency.
3. Repeat until one node remains:
  Pop two smallest-frequency nodes (X, Y).
  Create new internal node with frequency = X.freq + Y.freq, children X (left) and Y (right).
  Push new node back into heap.
4. The remaining node is the root of the Huffman tree.
5. Generate codes by traversing tree (0 = left, 1 = right). 
import heapq
from collections import Counter

class HuffmanNode:
 def __init__(self, char, freq, left=None, right=None):
 self.char = char # None for internal nodes
 self.freq = freq
 self.left = left
 self.right = right
 def __lt__(self, other):
 return self.freq < other.freq

def build_huffman(text):
 freqs = Counter(text)
 heap = [HuffmanNode(ch, f) for ch, f in freqs.items()]
 heapq.heapify(heap)

 while len(heap) > 1:
 a = heapq.heappop(heap)
 b = heapq.heappop(heap)
 merged = HuffmanNode(None, a.freq + b.freq, a, b)
 heapq.heappush(heap, merged)

 return heap[0] # root

def get_codes(node, prefix="", codes=None):
 if codes is None: codes = {}
 if node.char is not None: # leaf
 codes[node.char] = prefix or "0"
 return codes
 get_codes(node.left, prefix + "0", codes)
 get_codes(node.right, prefix + "1", codes)
 return codes

Worked example — building a Huffman tree

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Encode "ABRACADABRA"

Frequencies: A=5, B=2, R=2, C=1, D=1.

1
Heap: [(C, 1), (D, 1), (B, 2), (R, 2), (A, 5)].
2
Pop C(1), D(1) → merge to CD(2). Heap: [(CD, 2), (B, 2), (R, 2), (A, 5)].
3
Pop CD(2), B(2) → merge to CDB(4). Heap: [(R, 2), (A, 5), (CDB, 4)].
4
Pop R(2), CDB(4) → merge to R-CDB(6). Heap: [(A, 5), (R-CDB, 6)].
5
Pop A(5), R-CDB(6) → merge to root(11). Heap: [(root, 11)]. Done.
✓
Codes (one possible assignment): A=0, R=10, B=110, C=1110, D=1111.

Computing compression ratio

SIZE COMPARISON
Fixed-length (ASCII): each char = 8 bits.
  "ABRACADABRA" = 11 chars × 8 = 88 bits.

Huffman: sum (freq × code_length) for each char.
  A=5×1 + B=2×3 + R=2×2 + C=1×4 + D=1×4 = 5 + 6 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 23 bits.

Compression ratio: 23 / 88 ≈ 26% of original. Saved ~74%.

Optimal substructure of Huffman

WHY HUFFMAN IS OPTIMAL
Huffman's greedy choice (combining the two LEAST-frequent nodes) is provably optimal because:
  1. The two least-frequent characters MUST be siblings in some optimal tree (deepest leaves).
  2. Combining them and recursing yields an optimal tree for the smaller problem.
  3. Reversing the combination gives an optimal tree for the original.

Complexity

HUFFMAN COMPLEXITY
Time: O(n log n) where n = number of distinct characters.
  n−1 heap operations × O(log n) each.
Space: O(n) for the tree.

Encoding/decoding a text of length T: O(T) once the tree is built.

Where Huffman is used

HUFFMAN APPLICATIONS
JPEG: Huffman tables for DCT coefficients.
MP3: Huffman codes for compressed audio frames.
ZIP / GZIP / DEFLATE: Huffman + LZ77 sliding-window compression.
PNG: DEFLATE format = Huffman + LZ77.
HTTP/2: HPACK header compression uses Huffman.
BMP, GIF: variable-length codes (similar idea).
Text compression: any modern compressor includes Huffman as a stage.

Limitations

HUFFMAN'S LIMITS
Huffman gives one bit per character minimum — can't compress below the empirical entropy.
Doesn't exploit REPETITION (e.g., "the the the" — Huffman codes each "the" the same).
This is why production compressors combine Huffman with dictionary methods (LZ77, LZ78, LZW).

More advanced: arithmetic coding can break the 1-bit-per-char barrier.

Decoding Huffman codes

def decode(bits, root):
 """Decode a bit string using a Huffman tree."""
 result = []
 node = root
 for bit in bits:
 node = node.left if bit == "0" else node.right
 if node.char is not None: # leaf reached
 result.append(node.char)
 node = root
 return "".join(result)

Walk the tree from root; on '0' go left, on '1' go right; emit the leaf character when reached, then restart from root.

Other compression families

FamilyExamplesStrength
Variable-lengthHuffman, arithmeticFrequency-based
DictionaryLZ77, LZ78, LZWRepeated substrings
RLERun-length encodingLong runs of same value
Transform-basedDCT (JPEG), waveletLossy multimedia
CombinedDEFLATE (Huffman + LZ77)General-purpose
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Forgetting that Huffman codes must be PREFIX-FREE — no codeword can be a prefix of another.

Computing compression ratio against the wrong baseline — compare to fixed-length (8 bits/char) for ASCII text.

Forgetting to ALSO send the tree (decoder needs it) — overhead can negate savings on small files.

Treating Huffman as compressing repeated patterns — that's LZ77's job. Huffman handles single-character frequency.

Building the tree with a wrong tie-breaking rule — multiple valid Huffman trees may exist, all optimal in TOTAL bits but with different code assignments.

★ ON THE OA

"Build a Huffman tree from these frequencies" → repeatedly merge two smallest.

"Generate Huffman codes from the tree" → traverse: 0 = left, 1 = right.

"Compute compression ratio" → sum(freq × code_length) ÷ (total_chars × 8).

"Why is Huffman optimal?" → greedy choice property + optimal substructure.

"Huffman complexity?" → O(n log n) where n = distinct characters.

"Where is Huffman used?" → ZIP, JPEG, MP3, HTTP/2 HPACK.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Huffman = optimal variable-length prefix encoding
  • Build via min-heap: repeatedly merge two least-frequent nodes
  • Codes from tree: 0 = left, 1 = right
  • Compression: fewer bits for common chars, more for rare
  • Provably optimal among prefix codes (greedy works here)
  • Time: O(n log n) where n = distinct characters
  • Used in: ZIP, JPEG, MP3, HTTP/2, PNG (via DEFLATE)
  • Doesn't exploit repetition — combined with LZ77 for full compression
★ ON THE OA / PA — WATCH FOR

Huffman coding = greedy, builds a prefix-free binary tree by repeatedly merging the two lowest-frequency nodes → frequent symbols get shorter codes (lossless compression). OA: it's greedy and produces optimal prefix codes.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
freqs A:5 B:2 C:1  -> merge C+B(3) -> merge (3)+A(8)
shorter codes for higher frequency

Result: greedy → optimal prefix code

Merging the two rarest nodes each step yields the minimum-weighted-path tree, giving optimal prefix codes — a classic greedy proof the OA references.

String matching is the search problem at the heart of grep, find-and-replace, search engines, plagiarism detection, DNA sequence analysis, and intrusion detection. The OA tests recognizing the two main strategies (naive O(nm) vs KMP O(n+m)) and explaining why preprocessing matters. Even though string matching doesn't appear in the Parcel Service PA, it's a foundational algorithm pattern.

The string matching problem

PROBLEM STATEMENT
Given a TEXT T of length n and a PATTERN P of length m (m ≤ n), find:
  Does P occur in T? (existence)
  Where does P occur? (location)
  How many times does P occur? (count)
  All occurrences? (enumeration)

Pattern P could be a word, regex, file signature, DNA subsequence, etc.

Naive string matching

def naive_search(text, pattern):
 """Brute-force string search. Returns first match index or -1."""
 n, m = len(text), len(pattern)
 for i in range(n - m + 1):
 match = True
 for j in range(m):
 if text[i + j] != pattern[j]:
 match = False
 break
 if match:
 return i
 return -1
NAIVE COMPLEXITY
Outer loop: n − m + 1 starting positions.
Inner loop: up to m comparisons per position.

Worst case: O(n · m).
Best case: O(n) when first character mismatches every time.

Adversarial input (text = "aaaa...a", pattern = "aaaa...ab"): always matches m−1 characters before mismatching → O(n · m).

Why naive is slow — the redundant work

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Naive on adversarial input

Text = "AAAAAB" (n=6), Pattern = "AAAB" (m=4).

i=0
Compare AAAA vs AAAB → match A, A, A, then mismatch at B vs B? Wait — text has A here. Compare AAAA-vs-AAAB: A=A, A=A, A=A, A≠B. 4 comparisons, mismatch.
📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
i=1
Compare AAAB vs AAAB: A=A, A=A, A=A, B=B. Match found at index 1!
⚠
Naive RECHECKED characters at positions 1, 2, 3 even though the previous attempt already matched them. KMP avoids this.

KMP — Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm

KMP IDEA
Preprocess the PATTERN to build a "failure function" (a.k.a. LPS array — Longest Proper Prefix that is also Suffix).
When a mismatch occurs, the failure function tells you how far to slide the pattern WITHOUT rechecking already-matched characters.

Result: each character of the text is examined at most twice. Total: O(n + m).

The failure function (LPS array)

LPS DEFINITION
For pattern P of length m: LPS[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of P[0..i] that's also a suffix of P[0..i].

"Proper" = not equal to the entire string itself.

Used to know "if we matched i characters and then mismatched, we already know the next LPS[i-1] characters match somewhere — skip ahead."
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — LPS for "ABABCABAB"

Compute LPS[i] for each prefix length:

iP[0..i]LPSMeaning
0A0single char, no proper prefix
1AB0no overlap
2ABA1"A" is prefix and suffix
3ABAB2"AB" is prefix and suffix
4ABABC0C breaks it
5ABABCA1"A"
6ABABCAB2"AB"
7ABABCABA3"ABA"
8ABABCABAB4"ABAB"

KMP implementation

def compute_lps(pattern):
 """Compute LPS array for KMP. O(m)."""
 m = len(pattern)
 lps = [0] * m
 length = 0
 i = 1
 while i < m:
 if pattern[i] == pattern[length]:
 length += 1
 lps[i] = length
 i += 1
 else:
 if length != 0:
 length = lps[length - 1]
 else:
 lps[i] = 0
 i += 1
 return lps

def kmp_search(text, pattern):
 """Find first occurrence of pattern in text via KMP. O(n + m)."""
 if not pattern: return 0
 lps = compute_lps(pattern)
 n, m = len(text), len(pattern)
 i = j = 0
 while i < n:
 if text[i] == pattern[j]:
 i += 1; j += 1
 if j == m:
 return i - j # match found
 else:
 if j != 0:
 j = lps[j - 1] # use LPS to skip ahead
 else:
 i += 1
 return -1
KMP COMPLEXITY
Preprocessing: O(m) to build LPS.
Searching: O(n) — each text character examined ≤ 2 times.
Total: O(n + m).

Vs naive O(n · m): for n = 1,000,000 and m = 100, KMP is ~100× faster on adversarial input.

Boyer-Moore — practical winner

BOYER-MOORE
Compares pattern to text RIGHT-TO-LEFT.
On mismatch, uses two heuristics:
  Bad character heuristic: skip ahead based on the mismatched character.
  Good suffix heuristic: skip ahead based on previously-matched suffix.

Average case: O(n / m) — SUBLINEAR! Faster as the pattern grows.
Used by: grep, vim, most text editor "find" implementations.

Rabin-Karp — hashing approach

RABIN-KARP
Hash the pattern. Slide a window over the text, hashing each window of length m.
Compare hashes; only do char-by-char comparison on hash matches.
Uses ROLLING HASH — update hash in O(1) when window slides.

Best for MULTI-PATTERN search: hash all patterns, look for any hash match.
Used in: plagiarism detection, file deduplication, version-control diffs.

Regular expressions — generalized matching

REGEX
A pattern language describing a SET of strings.
Standard tools: Python's re, grep, sed, awk.

Implementation: regex compiles to a finite automaton (NFA or DFA).
Worst case: O(n · m) for backtracking implementations; O(n) for proper Thompson NFA.
Some regex features (back-references) make matching NP-hard.

Real-world string matching applications

USE CASES
grep, search: find text in files (Boyer-Moore in GNU grep).
Editor find/replace: text editors use Boyer-Moore or KMP.
DNA / protein sequence matching: BLAST, BWA use suffix arrays.
Plagiarism detection: Rabin-Karp for fingerprinting documents.
Web search engines: inverted indexes + various string algorithms.
Intrusion detection: Aho-Corasick for matching many attack signatures.
Spam filtering: matching against keyword lists.
Spell checking: edit distance + dictionary matching.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Saying "KMP is always faster than naive" — only on adversarial input. For random text, naive is often competitive.

Confusing "longest common substring" (separate problem, harder) with "find pattern in text."

Forgetting that Boyer-Moore's worst case is also O(n·m) — it's fast on AVERAGE.

Using regex when a simple substring search would do — slower and more error-prone.

For multi-pattern: running KMP m times for m patterns. Use Aho-Corasick instead.

★ ON THE OA

"Naive search complexity?" → O(n · m) worst case.

"What does KMP improve?" → eliminates redundant comparisons via LPS preprocessing.

"KMP complexity?" → O(n + m).

"What's the LPS array?" → longest proper prefix that's also a suffix at each position.

"Best practical algorithm?" → Boyer-Moore (used by grep, editors).

"Multi-pattern search?" → Aho-Corasick.

"Pattern matching with hashing?" → Rabin-Karp.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Naive search: O(n · m) worst — slow on adversarial input
  • KMP: O(n + m) via LPS array preprocessing
  • LPS = longest proper prefix that's also a suffix
  • Boyer-Moore: O(n / m) average — fastest in practice
  • Rabin-Karp: rolling hash, great for multi-pattern
  • Aho-Corasick: many patterns at once (grep, IDS)
  • Real uses: grep, editors, BLAST, plagiarism detection, IDS
  • Regex generalizes string matching to pattern languages
★ ON THE OA / PA — WATCH FOR

Naive string matching is O(n·m); KMP is O(n+m) using a prefix table to skip re-checks; Rabin-Karp uses hashing for average O(n+m). OA: KMP avoids re-examining characters via the failure/prefix function.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
naive: at each of n positions, compare up to m chars
KMP: precompute prefix table -> never backtrack in text

Result: KMP O(n+m) vs naive O(nm)

KMP's prefix table records how far to shift on a mismatch so the text pointer never moves backward — the source of its linear time.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

NP-completeness is one of the deepest ideas in computer science — it explains WHY some problems (TSP, knapsack, SAT) seem impossible to solve efficiently. For the Parcel Service PA, this section justifies WHY you used a heuristic (nearest-neighbor) instead of an exact algorithm: TSP is NP-hard, so brute-force solutions are infeasible past tiny inputs. The OA tests recognition of P, NP, NP-complete, NP-hard, and the implications for algorithm design.

P — problems we can solve fast

CLASS P (Polynomial)
Decision problems solvable in POLYNOMIAL TIME (O(n^k) for some constant k).

Examples:
  Sorting: O(n log n)
  Shortest path (Dijkstra): O((V+E) log V)
  MST: O(E log V)
  Matching in bipartite graphs: O(V·E)
  String matching (KMP): O(n + m)

P is generally considered "tractable" — feasible to solve at scale.

NP — problems we can verify fast

CLASS NP (Nondeterministic Polynomial)
Decision problems where a CANDIDATE SOLUTION can be VERIFIED in polynomial time.

We may not know how to FIND the solution efficiently, but given one we can CHECK it fast.

Examples:
  Sudoku: easy to verify a candidate grid; hard to find one.
  TSP: easy to check if a tour ≤ K; hard to find one.
  3-SAT: easy to check a truth assignment; hard to find one.

Note: P ⊆ NP (if you can solve fast, you can verify fast — just solve it).

NP-complete — the hardest in NP

NP-COMPLETE
Problems in NP that are AS HARD AS any problem in NP.

Formally: every NP problem can be REDUCED in polynomial time to an NP-complete problem.

If you find a polynomial algorithm for ANY NP-complete problem, you've solved them ALL — proving P = NP (worth $1M Clay Millennium prize).

No one has done this in 50+ years. Most CS researchers believe P ≠ NP.

Famous NP-complete problems

CLASSIC NP-COMPLETE
3-SAT: satisfiability of Boolean formulas with 3 literals per clause.
TSP (decision version): is there a tour of length ≤ K?
Hamilton cycle: does the graph have a Hamiltonian cycle?
Subset sum: is there a subset summing to exactly K?
Knapsack (decision): can we fit items of total value ≥ V in weight ≤ W?
Graph coloring: can the graph be k-colored?
Vertex cover: is there a set of ≤ K vertices covering all edges?
Clique: is there a complete subgraph of size ≥ K?
Set cover: cover all elements with ≤ K subsets?

NP-hard — at least as hard as NP-complete

NP-HARD
At least as hard as NP-complete problems, but possibly NOT IN NP.

Examples:
  TSP optimization (find SHORTEST tour, not just "is there one ≤ K?")
  Halting problem (NOT in NP — undecidable!)
  Optimization versions of NP-complete problems

Optimization is "harder" than decision: knowing a tour exists is easy to verify; finding the SHORTEST takes longer to certify.

The Traveling Salesman Problem

TSP — TWO VERSIONS
Decision: given a graph and number K, is there a tour visiting all vertices with total weight ≤ K? — NP-COMPLETE.
Optimization: find the SHORTEST tour. — NP-HARD.

Both: no known polynomial algorithm; brute force is O(n!).

Why TSP is hard

COMBINATORIAL EXPLOSION
n cities → (n−1)!/2 distinct tours.

  n = 10: 181,440 tours — instant.
  n = 15: 43,589,145,600 tours — minutes.
  n = 20: 6 × 10¹⁶ tours — millennia.
  n = 40 (Parcel Service): 10⁴⁷ tours — hopelessly infeasible.

Even with Held-Karp DP at O(n² · 2^n): n = 40 means 4 × 10¹⁴ cells. Still infeasible.

How to handle NP-hard problems in practice

FIVE STRATEGIES
1. Heuristics: fast approximate algorithms (NN for TSP, greedy for set cover).
2. Approximation algorithms: heuristics with PROVEN bounds (Christofides for metric TSP: ≤ 1.5× optimal).
3. Branch and bound: smart pruning of the search space.
4. Restricted versions: solve special cases efficiently (TSP on planar graphs is easier).
5. Metaheuristics: simulated annealing, genetic algorithms — practical for moderate n.

The P vs NP question

P =? NP
THE most famous open problem in CS.

IF P = NP: every problem with a fast checker has a fast solver. Cryptography breaks (RSA depends on factoring being hard). Drug discovery, scheduling, AI optimization all become trivial.

IF P ≠ NP (the consensus belief): some problems are inherently harder to solve than to verify. Hard problems require either heuristics, approximations, or exponential time.

$1M prize for resolving the question (Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Problems).

Reductions — the technical heart of NP-completeness

POLYNOMIAL-TIME REDUCTION
Problem A REDUCES to problem B if you can convert any instance of A into an instance of B in polynomial time, such that the solution to B yields the solution to A.

If A reduces to B and B is in P, then A is in P.
If A reduces to B and A is NP-hard, then B is NP-hard.

Cook-Levin theorem (1971): 3-SAT is NP-complete. Every other NP-complete proof is a reduction from 3-SAT (or from another already-known NP-complete problem).

Parcel Service Section D / F language for the PA

PA WRITE-UP TEMPLATE
"The Parcel Service routing problem is a constrained Traveling Salesman Problem. TSP is NP-HARD — no known polynomial-time algorithm exists, and brute-force enumeration is O(n!). For the 16-package per-truck limit, this is 16! = 2 × 10¹³ permutations, infeasible to compute.

Held-Karp dynamic programming (O(n² · 2^n)) reduces this for small n but still exceeds practical limits past n ≈ 25.

Polynomial-time HEURISTICS — nearest-neighbor (O(n²)), 2-opt local search, simulated annealing, genetic algorithms — produce good (but not optimal) routes. For Parcel Service, NN yields routes well under the 140-mile constraint, satisfying the requirement.

IF a polynomial algorithm for TSP existed, P would equal NP — a $1M open problem in computer science. Until then, heuristics remain the practical choice."

Other interesting hard problems

BEYOND NP
PSPACE-complete: solvable in polynomial SPACE (memory) — superset of NP. Generalized chess, Go.
EXPTIME: requires exponential TIME. Some game-tree problems.
Undecidable: NO algorithm exists at all. Halting problem, equivalence of two programs.

The complexity hierarchy goes much deeper than P vs NP.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKES

Saying "NP" means "Not Polynomial" — wrong. NP = "Nondeterministic Polynomial" (verifiable in polynomial time).

Calling all hard problems "NP-complete" — most production hard problems are NP-HARD, not NP-complete.

Treating P = NP as proven false — it's an OPEN question. Most believe P ≠ NP but no proof.

Saying "TSP is unsolvable" — it IS solvable, just not efficiently for large n.

Confusing NP-complete (hardest in NP) with NP-hard (at least as hard as NP, possibly outside NP).

Attempting brute-force TSP on n > 15 — not happening on Earth's compute.

★ ON THE OA

"What's P?" → polynomial-time solvable.

"What's NP?" → polynomial-time verifiable.

"NP-complete vs NP-hard?" → NP-complete: in NP and as hard as any NP problem. NP-hard: at least as hard, possibly not in NP.

"Is TSP NP-hard?" → YES.

"Why use NN for Parcel Service?" → TSP is NP-hard; NN is polynomial heuristic.

"Famous NP-complete problems?" → 3-SAT, Hamilton, knapsack, vertex cover, graph coloring.

"P =? NP" → open; widely believed P ≠ NP.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • P: solvable in polynomial time
  • NP: verifiable in polynomial time
  • NP-complete: in NP AND as hard as any NP problem (3-SAT, TSP-decision, etc.)
  • NP-hard: at least as hard as NP-complete; possibly not in NP (TSP-optimization)
  • P =? NP is an open $1M question — most believe P ≠ NP
  • NP-hard problems handled by: heuristics, approximations, branch-and-bound, special cases
  • TSP brute force = O(n!); Held-Karp = O(n²·2^n); both infeasible past tiny n
  • For Parcel Service PA: cite TSP NP-hardness as justification for nearest-neighbor heuristic
★ ON THE OA / PA — WATCH FOR

NP-complete = verifiable in polynomial time, no known polynomial solution; TSP (decision) is NP-complete. That's why the PA uses a HEURISTIC (nearest-neighbor), not an exact optimum. OA: recognize NP-complete problems and P vs NP basics.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE
exact TSP for n cities: ~ (n-1)!/2 routes
10 cities -> 181,440 routes; grows factorially

Result: exact TSP infeasible → use heuristics

Factorial route growth makes exact TSP impractical, so real systems (and the PA) accept near-optimal heuristic routes. Know why NP-hardness forces this.

Why nearest-neighbor is the right pick

The Parcel Service routing problem is a constrained Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP). TSP is NP-hard, so we can't compute optimal in reasonable time. We need a heuristic. The standard recommended choice is nearest-neighbor (NN):

WHY NEAREST-NEIGHBOR FOR Parcel Service
✓ Simple to implement (low risk of bugs)
✓ Produces good-enough routes — easily under 140 miles for the Parcel Service data
✓ Time complexity O(n²) — fast for n = 40
✓ Easy to explain in the write-up
✓ Well-known / accepted by evaluators
✓ Easy to extend with deadline-priority logic

Trade-off: not OPTIMAL (could be 10-30% over optimal). For 140-mile constraint, doesn't matter.

Nearest-neighbor pseudocode (use this in Section C1)

FUNCTION nearest_neighbor(truck, package_list, distance_matrix):
 current_location = HUB_ADDRESS
 route = [current_location]
 total_distance = 0

 WHILE package_list is not empty:
 nearest_package = NULL
 nearest_distance = INFINITY

 FOR each package in package_list:
 d = distance_matrix[current_location][package.address]
 IF d < nearest_distance:
 nearest_distance = d
 nearest_package = package

 # Travel to nearest package
 total_distance = total_distance + nearest_distance
 current_location = nearest_package.address
 route.append(current_location)

 # Mark delivered, update timestamps
 nearest_package.delivery_time = current_time
 nearest_package.status = DELIVERED
 package_list.remove(nearest_package)

 # Return to hub
 total_distance = total_distance + distance_matrix[current_location][HUB_ADDRESS]
 RETURN route, total_distance

Outer loop: n iterations (one per remaining package).
Inner loop: scans all remaining packages → up to n.
Each iteration: O(n) to find nearest → O(n²) total.

For n = 16 (max packages per truck): 256 distance comparisons per truck. Trivially fast.

Distance lookup: O(1) (matrix lookup).
Hash table operations: O(1) average for insert/lookup/update.

Overall algorithm: O(n²)
SPACE COMPLEXITY
Distance matrix: O(V²) where V = 27 addresses.
Package hash table: O(n) where n = 40 packages.
Route per truck: O(n).

Overall: O(V² + n)

The custom hash table is the SECOND most important code component (after routing) and the most-failed-on requirement. The rubric explicitly calls for a "self-adjusting data structure" — this is your hash table. Using Python's dict, even wrapped in a class, will be flagged. This section walks you through implementing a chaining hash table from scratch and wiring it into the Parcel Service app.

Why "self-adjusting"?

RUBRIC LANGUAGE
Section C6 asks for a "self-adjusting data structure." The intent: a hash table that resizes when the load factor crosses a threshold (typically 0.75).

Insertion may trigger a RESIZE → all buckets get rehashed into a larger array.

Even if you don't actually implement resize logic, you can SIMULATE it (start with capacity 40 and discuss how to grow if needed). Many students just use 40 buckets fixed and explain the resize logic in the write-up.

The HashTable class — full Python skeleton

class HashTable:
 """
 Custom hash table using chaining.
 Stores Package objects keyed by package ID.
 """

 def __init__(self, initial_capacity=40):
 self.capacity = initial_capacity
 self.size = 0
 # Each bucket is a list (chain) of [key, value] pairs
 self.buckets = [[] for _ in range(initial_capacity)]

 def _hash(self, key):
 """Simple hash: package ID modulo capacity."""
 return int(key) % self.capacity

 def insert(self, key, value):
 """Insert or update. O(1) average, O(n) worst-case."""
 bucket_index = self._hash(key)
 bucket = self.buckets[bucket_index]
 # Check if key already exists; update if so
 for kv in bucket:
 if kv[0] == key:
 kv[1] = value
 return
 # New key — append to bucket
 bucket.append([key, value])
 self.size += 1
 # Optional: resize if load factor > 0.75
 if self.size / self.capacity > 0.75:
 self._resize()

 def lookup(self, key):
 """Return value for key, or None. O(1) average, O(n) worst-case."""
 bucket_index = self._hash(key)
 bucket = self.buckets[bucket_index]
 for kv in bucket:
 if kv[0] == key:
 return kv[1]
 return None

 def remove(self, key):
 """Remove a key. O(1) average."""
 bucket_index = self._hash(key)
 bucket = self.buckets[bucket_index]
 for i, kv in enumerate(bucket):
 if kv[0] == key:
 bucket.pop(i)
 self.size -= 1
 return True
 return False

 def _resize(self):
 """Double capacity and rehash all entries."""
 old_buckets = self.buckets
 self.capacity *= 2
 self.size = 0
 self.buckets = [[] for _ in range(self.capacity)]
 for bucket in old_buckets:
 for kv in bucket:
 self.insert(kv[0], kv[1])

 def all_packages(self):
 """Iterate over all packages — useful for displays."""
 for bucket in self.buckets:
 for kv in bucket:
 yield kv[1]

The Package class

class Package:
 def __init__(self, package_id, address, city, state, zip_code,
 deadline, weight, notes):
 self.id = package_id
 self.address = address
 self.city = city
 self.state = state
 self.zip = zip_code
 self.deadline = deadline # e.g., "9:00 AM" or "EOD"
 self.weight = weight
 self.notes = notes
 # Tracking fields:
 self.status = "AT_HUB" # AT_HUB, EN_ROUTE, DELIVERED
 self.truck_id = None
 self.departed_hub_time = None
 self.delivered_time = None

 def update_status(self, query_time):
 """Return status string for a given query time."""
 if self.delivered_time and query_time >= self.delivered_time:
 return f"Delivered at {self.delivered_time}"
 if self.departed_hub_time and query_time >= self.departed_hub_time:
 return f"En route on truck {self.truck_id}"
 return "At hub"

 def __repr__(self):
 return f"Package({self.id}, {self.address}, deadline={self.deadline})"

import csv

def load_packages(filename, hash_table):
 """Read package CSV and insert into hash table."""
 with open(filename, 'r') as f:
 reader = csv.reader(f)
 next(reader) # skip header if present
 for row in reader:
 package_id = int(row[0])

 package = Package(package_id, address, city, state, zip_code,
 deadline, weight, notes)
 hash_table.insert(package_id, package)
 return hash_table

A* search and admissible heuristics

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A* finds a shortest path by being smart about which node to expand next. It combines the known cost so far with an estimate of the cost remaining, so it heads toward the goal instead of exploring blindly.

THE A* EVALUATION FUNCTION
f(n) = g(n) + h(n) — where g(n) = actual cost from start to n, and h(n) = heuristic estimate of cost from n to the goal. A* always expands the node with the smallest f.
⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Admissible heuristic: never overestimates the true remaining cost (h(n) ≤ actual). With an admissible h, A* is guaranteed to find an optimal (shortest) path.

Consistent (monotonic): h(n) ≤ cost(n,n') + h(n') for every neighbor. Consistency implies admissibility and lets A* skip re-expanding nodes.

Straight-line (Euclidean) distance is a classic admissible heuristic for maps — it never exceeds the real road distance.

WORKED EXAMPLE — A* vs its cousins
AlgorithmExpands byUses heuristic?
Dijkstrag(n) onlyNo (h=0)
Greedy best-firsth(n) onlyYes, but ignores cost so far
A*f(n)=g(n)+h(n)Yes, balanced

A* with h=0 becomes Dijkstra; A* using only h is greedy best-first.

📝 EXAM WORDING

f = g + h. Admissible = never overestimates → guarantees optimal path. Consistent = triangle-inequality condition, stronger than admissible. A* with h = 0 is exactly Dijkstra.

🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
What makes a heuristic admissible?
  1. It always overestimates
  2. It never overestimates the true remaining cost
  3. It equals g(n)
  4. It ignores the goal
Show answer
B. Admissible means h(n) ≤ actual cost to goal — never an overestimate — which guarantees A* optimality.

Design Paradigms at a Glance

Three paradigms dominate advanced design. Greedy makes a locally optimal choice and never reconsiders; it is correct only when the problem exhibits the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure. Divide-and-conquer (D&C) splits into independent subproblems, recurses, and combines. Dynamic programming (DP) applies when subproblems overlap; it memoizes to avoid recomputation.

💡 KEY RESULTS
  • 0/1 knapsack: DP in O(nW) — pseudo-polynomial, exponential in input bits of W.
  • LCS / edit distance: O(mn) time, O(min(m,n)) space with rolling arrays.
  • Matrix-chain order: O(n^3) DP over interval lengths.
⚙️ FORMULAS

Master theorem for T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n), compare f with n^(log_b a): smaller → Θ(n^log_b a); equal (×log^k n) → Θ(n^log_b a · log^(k+1) n); larger (regular) → Θ(f(n)).

Knapsack: K[i][w]=max(K[i-1][w], v_i+K[i-1][w-w_i]). Edit: D[i][j]=min(D[i-1][j]+1, D[i][j-1]+1, D[i-1][j-1]+[a_i≠b_j]).

📝 TECHNIQUE

Prove greedy optimal by an exchange argument: transform any optimal solution toward the greedy one without increasing cost. Define DP by naming the subproblem, writing the recurrence, then the evaluation order (bottom-up or memoized top-down).

⚠️ SUBTLETY

Greedy fails on 0/1 knapsack and on coin systems that are not canonical (e.g. {1,3,4} for 6). Weighted interval scheduling needs DP, not the earliest-finish greedy that solves the unweighted case.

📖 Worked example — a hard graph/hashing problem, start to finish

WORKED EXAMPLE — Dijkstra, traced on a small graph
Graph: A→B (4), A→C (1), C→B (2), B→D (5), C→D (8). Shortest A→D?

Start: dist = {A:0, B:∞, C:∞, D:∞}.
1. Visit A: relax neighbors → B = 4, C = 1.
2. Visit C (smallest dist 1): B = min(4, 1+2) = 3, D = 1+8 = 9.
3. Visit B (dist 3): D = min(9, 3+5) = 8.
4. Visit D → done. Shortest path A→C→B→D, cost 8.

The discipline: always expand the UNVISITED node with the smallest tentative distance, and relax = “is going through me cheaper?” The greedy pick + relax loop is the whole algorithm — and the WGUPS routing project is this idea plus a hash table for package lookup.
⚠️ DIJKSTRA FORBIDS NEGATIVE EDGES
With a negative edge weight the greedy “smallest first” assumption breaks (Bellman-Ford handles that case). And in the project context: the package hash table’s O(1) lookup is what keeps the route loop fast.

Graphs, Hashing, and WGUPS Routing

Dijkstra finds single-source shortest paths on non-negative weights greedily with a priority queue; Bellman-Ford tolerates negative edges and detects negative cycles by relaxing all edges V−1 times. MST algorithms exploit the cut property: the lightest edge crossing any cut is safe.

💡 KEY RESULTS
  • Dijkstra (binary heap): O((V+E) log V); Bellman-Ford: O(VE).
  • Kruskal: O(E log E) with union-find; Prim (heap): O(E log V).
  • Topological sort: O(V+E), valid only on a DAG.
  • Chained hash search: average O(1+λ) where λ=n/m.
⚙️ FORMULAS

Load factor λ = n/m (items/buckets). A* uses f(n)=g(n)+h(n). Admissible: h(n) ≤ h*(n). Consistent: h(u) ≤ c(u,v)+h(v).

📝 TECHNIQUE

WGUPS uses nearest-neighbor greedy routing: from the current stop repeatedly pick the closest un-visited address via a distance matrix, plus a custom chaining hash table keyed on package ID for O(1) average lookup and O(1) amortized insert.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

A consistent heuristic is always admissible, but admissible does not imply consistent. Nearest-neighbor for TSP has no constant approximation ratio in general. Dijkstra can fail with even a single negative edge because a settled node may still be improvable.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.
